Teenagers say social media is about more than scrolling, with platforms increasingly central to friendships and communication. Photo / 123rf

They spend hours scrolling, message their parents on Snapchat and admit they have already seen things online they wish they hadn’t. But as politicians push to lock under-16s out of social media, the teenagers who would be banned have a message for rule-makers. Rachel Maher speaks to 14- and 15-year-olds about what a social media ban would mean for them.

Teenagers facing the prospect of being locked out of social media say a ban could change more than their screen time.

National is pushing for restrictions that would prevent children under 16 from holding social media accounts, with platforms expected to take responsibility for verifying users’ ages.

National MP Catherine Wedd’s Social Media (Age-Restricted Users) Bill was drawn from the members’ ballot in October 2025, and a parliamentary inquiry has since recommended that New Zealand restrict under-16 access and strengthen regulation of online platforms.

The Government has been developing its own approach, with National aiming to introduce legislation and secure its passage before the 2026 election, although exactly how age verification and enforcement would work remains under development.

For five Tauranga Boys’ College students, social media is not simply somewhere to waste an afternoon scrolling.

It is where friendships are maintained, plans are made, problems are shared and, for some, where they find the space to say things they struggle to voice elsewhere.

The boys estimate they spend between two and six hours a day on social media, using everything from Instagram and Snapchat to Discord, YouTube and Facebook.

Boy 1, who spends five to six hours a day online, said Instagram allowed him to meet people with similar interests and experiences.

He believed restrictions would represent a “really big shift” in his life.

“Social media has been like a really good thing for me because I can tell other people about my problems.

“I can’t really talk to other people about like same interests, like relatable problems that we have.”

Boy 2, who estimated he spent four to five hours a day online, said Snapchat was a way of talking to friends and questioned how teenagers would organise their lives without it.

“What are you going to do to connect, make plans with other people and organise things if you can’t communicate without meeting someone in person?”

For Boy 3, the issue went deeper than boredom or convenience.

He said social media provided a “safe space” to discuss his emotions with friends when he did not always feel able to have those conversations at home.

“If social media was banned, I would probably start deteriorating in that sense because I’d only have the time I spend in life with friends, like at school, to actually be able to vent and explain my problems.”

The boys believed adults could overlook the meaningful conversations occurring behind the hours of scrolling and messaging.

Boy 1 said social media had helped him through “a lot of hard times”, while Boy 3 worried restrictions could cut teenagers off from friends they trusted.

“If that gets taken away from them, I feel like it’ll cause a lot more harm than good.”

But none of the boys pretended social media was harmless.

They had encountered scams, misinformation, bullying, nudity, racism and homophobic abuse.

Boy 4 said he had been added to Snapchat group chats where people shared nudity, bullied and harassed others, and had seen students use TikTok to mock teachers and classmates.

“I think it’s very bad because it’s just basically bullying people.”

Boy 3 said he had become “desensitised” after years of encountering inappropriate material and misinformation.

Boy 5 acknowledged harmful aspects, but said banning social media could create new problems.

“Nothing’s ever perfect.”

And if restrictions arrived, the boys were sceptical they would keep teenagers offline for long.

They rattled off workarounds: VPNs (virtual private networks), alternative accounts and false birthdays.

“You could probably use a search engine and search how to get past it,” Boy 2 said.

“You can basically ask AI, and it would tell you how.”

Even if there was no way around the restrictions, Boy 2 doubted he would suddenly abandon his phone.

“I’d still be on my phone. It wouldn’t make me want to go outside more.”

For a group of St Hilda’s Collegiate School students, the prospect of life without social media prompted everything from practical objections to something approaching horror.

“Hell no,” Girl 2 said. “The day social media dies is the day I die.”

All eight girls said they spent at least three hours a day on various social media platforms, while some admitted weekend “doomscrolling” could stretch towards 10 hours.

Girl 1 said she was essentially online all day during the weekends, from waking around 8am until going to sleep around midnight.

But despite that heavy use, the girls were largely unconvinced that proposed restrictions for under-16s would keep teenagers off social media.

“A lot of people already fake their age on social media,” Girl 1 said.

“If social media gets banned for under-16s, they’re still going to do it anyway.”

VPNs were repeatedly suggested as an obvious workaround.

Girl 2 said students already used them to bypass restrictions blocking Snapchat, TikTok and other sites at school and during prep time at the hostel.

“We just put a VPN on, and then it works, and we sit there and scroll on TikTok.”

For the girls, social media was deeply embedded in how teenagers communicated.

“No one texts on messages unless you’re texting, like, old people,” Girl 2 said.

“I even text my mum on Snapchat. We have a streak.”

Girl 3 said adults underestimated how central social media had become to young people’s friendships.

“Adults don’t know how hard it is and how social media’s literally our lives.

“We get to keep up with all our friends.”

Girl 4 said platforms such as Snapchat also made it easier to stay connected with people met through sports and other activities, where swapping a Snapchat username felt more natural than exchanging phone numbers.

But the girls acknowledged their relationship with social media was complicated.

Girl 8 said it could encourage creativity through cooking, baking and fashion content, while also meaning teenagers spent less time physically with friends.

Girl 7 believed removing social media could push her towards more hobbies and sport – but noted that she also used TikTok to learn guitar.

She questioned whether banning social media would eliminate bullying.

“If there wasn’t social media, people wouldn’t bully online; they’d bully in person, which would be worse.”

Several had been on social media since primary school, with some joining during the Covid-19 pandemic and one recalling getting Snapchat in 2018.

Asked what might fill the hours if the platforms suddenly disappeared, Girl 5 said she would “stare at the wall”.

“I would pick up some other unhealthy habit. Maybe I would pick up vaping, I don’t know.”

Rachel Maher is the education correspondent for the New Zealand Herald. She also covers other topics such as Auckland issues, crime and local government. She started at the Herald as a breaking news journalist in 2022, before joining the Auckland team this year.

Election 2026: Act’s public service ‘reset’ includes removing ‘good employer’ requirements, enshrining ‘need, not race’

New Zealand Herald August 15, 2026

The Act Party is proposing to remove “good employer” requirements from public service legislation, while also prohibiting agencies from resourcing any cultural or spiritual practices in the workplace.

The party is today announcing how it plans to “reset” the public service around what it calls the “basic principles of equal treatment, individual freedom, political and religious neutrality, and accountability for results”.

The election proposals go further than the reforms the coalition Government has already made to public service legislation, which included repealing provisions to promote diversity and inclusiveness.

“To unlock New Zealand’s potential we need one law for all, and one future together,” leader David Seymour said. “That starts with a public service that treats people as individuals, hires the best people for the job, and delivers services according to need.”

On the chopping block under Act is Section 73 of the Public Service Act, which requires the chief executives of Government departments to operate an employment policy that complies “with the principle of being a good employer”.

According to the legislation, to be a “good employer” is to have a policy “containing provisions generally accepted as necessary for the fair and proper treatment of employees in all aspects of their employment”.

These are listed as including “the impartial selection of suitably qualified people for appointment”, “good and safe working conditions”, and “an equal employment opportunities programme”.

It also mentions recognising the “employment requirements” of certain groups, like Māori, women, and people with disabilities. The need for “greater involvement of Māori in the public service” is also listed.

A similar section found in the Crown Entities Act would also be repealed if Act got its way after the November 7 election.

Seymour said these sections contained “race-based hiring requirements”.

“The public service should have the same employment rules as any other business,” Seymour said.

“Health and safety, non-discrimination, and disability rights are already covered elsewhere in the law. Public service jobs should go to the best person for the job, regardless of race. Hiring and promotion should be based on merit, skills, experience, and what the role actually requires.”

Seymour told the Herald that Section 73 of the Public Service Act was “about the public service having its own agenda of social engineering for its own sake within the workplace, rather than the main purpose of delivering for the public”.

He said he was “proud” of what the Government had achieved with its changes, but the continued existence of Section 73 meant “we’ve got a lot further to go”.

Act would also legally enforce that public services base their delivery of services on “need, not race”. That’s currently laid out in a Cabinet circular – essentially a formal notice – but Act would put it into law.

“Agencies will be required by law to follow the principle, and decisions that breach it could be challenged through judicial review,” said Seymour. “If two New Zealanders have the same need, they should be entitled to the same treatment from Government.”

The circular, issued in September 2024, said the Government was “concerned that in the absence of clear expectations, agencies may use ethnic identity or other forms of personal identity as a proxy for need, and therefore a justification in itself for targeted services”.

The next step in Act’s plan is to prohibit public service agencies from “initiating or resourcing cultural or spiritual practices as part of the workplace”.

“Public servants will remain free to practise their own religion, culture, or traditions in their own time, with reasonable accommodation where appropriate,” Seymour said.

The Act leader said workers should not “be expected to take part in a prayer, karakia, or other spiritual practice because they work for the Government”.

“Taxpayers should not be required to fund staff time or other resources for employer-initiated spiritual activity either.”

There has previously been controversy over cultural practices – like karakia – being resourced at some government agencies.

Act would also remove “irrelevant cultural requirements from public service jobs”.

“A person applying to work for the Government should be judged on whether they can do the job, not their knowledge of particular cultural concepts, values, or worldviews unless there is a genuine occupational reason for doing so.

“Act will direct public service agencies to remove those requirements from job advertisements and position descriptions where they are not relevant to the role, through a clear letter of expectations to the Public Service Commissioner and a Cabinet circular.”

The party says these changes are an “immediate start”, but the problems with the public service legislation “go deeper”.

It is suggesting there could be a “future rewrite” or a “wider reset of the Public Service Act to ensure neutrality”.

The Herald asked Seymour how that desire for a neutral public service squared with Act’s policy to allow ministers to appoint chief executives and remove them for specified reasons, like non-performance or policy misalignment.

He said that in terms of political neutrality, a minister could “abuse that”, but they would “face a consequence” for doing so.

It was in a minister’s interest to “appoint someone that will be effective, just like another employer”, Seymour said.

“If you’re a minister appointing a chief executive and you appoint someone that you like, but is not good at the job, then you are going to very quickly get in trouble as a minister.”

However, when it came to “cultural and spiritual neutrality, right now there is no safeguard for a worker who wants to just go and do their job and not be forced to affirm beliefs or participate in rituals that they don’t actually want anything to do with”.

Jamie Ensor is the NZ Herald’s chief political reporter, based in the press gallery at Parliament. He was previously a TV reporter and digital producer in the Newshub press gallery office. He was a finalist in 2025 for Political Journalist of the Year at the Voyager Media Awards.

Kāinga Ora staff who donned full protective equipment and picked a lock to gain entry to a state house were hit by a strong smell of animal excrement, rotting food and general uncleanliness.

The squalid conditions that greeted Scott Tuapola, a senior housing manager, inside the Ōtara flat during an “ad hoc visit” in March were outlined in a recent Tenancy Tribunal decision.

It described the floors at the flat, tenanted by Shalin Shalvina Sharma, as caked with “dirt, filth and faeces”.

The decision did not explain the reason for the visit or why it was necessary to pick the lock.

Rubbish was stacked against the walls, inside wardrobes and throughout the kitchen and bathroom.

The back door had been broken and wouldn’t lock, while a broken window frame and rubbish made entry into the kitchen difficult.

The following month, Kāinga Ora sought to terminate the tenancy. Figures released by the agency show it ended 38 tenancies in the year to June because of a property’s poor condition.

Despite ignoring three previous notices for failing to keep the property in a reasonably clean and tidy condition, Sharma avoided eviction after the tribunal found a fourth notice had not yet expired, leaving time to remedy the breaches.

The case was adjourned, and in June, Sharma wrote to the tribunal seeking a three-month adjournment, saying she was in hospital and unable to attend a hearing.

The tribunal asked for medical evidence to support the request, but none was forthcoming.

Last month, Kāinga Ora staff visited again, this time with Sharma’s tenancy support worker, again wearing full protective equipment when entering the property.

They found the carpet and floors heavily soiled with dirt, animal excrement, food and pet food.

Photographs showed cardboard, clothing and towels spread across the floor and covered with food, spoiled food, animal feed and pet excrement.

Rubbish was strewn across the floors, stacked around rooms and against walls, and piled up in the garden.

The bathroom was dirty, and both the toilet and walls were stained.

According to the decision, the kitchen was filthy with food stains covering the oven, benchtop and cupboards. The sink was full of dishes. The floor was covered in rubbish, spoiled food, pet excrement, empty food packets and household waste.

The laundry window was broken, and the lawns were overgrown. Cats were seen at the property, although it was unclear from the decision whether pets were allowed.

The offensive odour remained, and the flat was deemed unsuitable for habitation.

Contact the Open Justice team

In a statement, Kāinga Ora said it could not comment on individual tenants or their properties.

Claire Baldwin, acting regional manager for Counties Manukau, said its role was to provide people with a stable, healthy, and safe home.

Baldwin said the agency expected tenants to meet their responsibilities in return by looking after their home, managing their rubbish appropriately and being considerate neighbours.

Baldwin acknowledged that there were times when tenants faced circumstances that made it difficult to look after their homes.

In these instances, the agency worked with tenants and connected them with support agencies, she said.

If a tenant refused to engage with them or the issues remained unresolved, Baldwin said the agency took steps under the Residential Tenancies Act.

Last month, adjudicator Melanie Feist ordered that Sharma’s tenancy be terminated and returned to Kāinga Ora immediately.

The decision noted Sharma had failed to remedy four breach notices and that the property’s condition was deteriorating.

Catherine Hutton is an Open Justice reporter, based in Wellington. She has worked as a journalist at the Waikato Times and RNZ. Most recently she was working as a media adviser at the Ministry of Justice.

Revealed: Name of nurse in student death case at mental health unit

New Zealand Herald August 15, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

By Jimmy Ellingham of RNZ

A name-suppression order for one of the nurses responsible for the care of a 21-year-old student who died by suicide at a mental health ward has lapsed.

Erica Hume died in May 2014 at Palmerston North Hospital, a death Coroner Matthew Bates ruled as preventable and could have been avoided if staff had correctly followed policies and procedures.

He also found staff were under pressure due to the high number of patients and that the ward’s physical environment wasn’t fit for purpose. A replacement ward opened last year.

During an inquest into the death in 2022, temporary name suppression orders covered healthcare workers. When the coroner’s ruling was released in June these orders lifted, except for one covering registered nurse Donna Jo-Anne Jones.

She was granted temporary suppression to allow her to consider an appeal against the coroner’s ruling against her application for suppression.

She had until 31 July to do this but the Coroner’s Court and the High Court have confirmed no application was received.

Erica Hume’s parents, Carey and Owen, said they were pleased to see the order lapse.

In a statement to RNZ, they said: “Open justice does require people to be named and applications for a permanent non-disclosure order should be declined if there is truly to be embedded change in mental healthcare within New Zealand.”

Coroner Bates’ ruling declining Jones’ application for suppression said she cited interests of justice and personal privacy in arguing her name should remain secret. The coroner has ruled the specifics of her argument are suppressed.

Jones, who could not be contacted, managed Erica Hume’s admission to the Palmerston North Hospital mental health ward, known as ward 21, on 6 May 2014 and nursed her that evening. Erica Hume died the next day.

The coroner found that despite Erica Hume’s care worker giving a “detailed and diligent verbal handover”, Jones did not take on board the heightened risk of suicide.

She also failed to adequately review admission information in Erica Hume’s clinical file and record that information on admission documentation.

Coroner Bates said: “These failures meant that from the time of admission to ward 21, Erica’s heightened risk of suicide... went either unrecognised on the ward or, at the very least, the severity of her risk was not appreciated.”

He said this affected the care Erica Hume received, including the levels of observation she was under, and the following shift wasn’t fully appraised of the situation.

The coroner said Jones believed she did the best she could in the time available, writing in Erica Hume’s file: “Admission paperwork to complete. Due to ward activity, unable to do.”

Jones did not alone bear responsibility for Erica Hume’s death and no individual was singled out for criticism in his findings, the coroner said.

He added: “The role she played occurred in the context of widespread systemic failings and resourcing shortfalls at ward 21, including prolonged staff shortages.”

Jones has been a registered nurse for almost 20 years and still works at Palmerston North Hospital.

Carey and Owen Hume said after Erica’s death they encountered a hospital system “embedded with non-disclosure” and a “deep-seated expectation of non-accountability”.

They said: “It is our opinion that accountability is a major factor in the examination of the care of Erica, and this includes the actions or inactions of all parties, staff and management.

“It is also our opinion that the purpose of having an inquest is to determine what happened and try to ensure that there is no repeat of the circumstances that allowed it to happen.

“This means, too, that individual as well as collective responsibility and accountability must occur.”

They said for too long it was assumed healthcare workers would receive name suppression because it would harm their therapeutic relationship with patients, which was a a poor excuse.

They added: “We firmly believe patients and families have the right to informed consent and knowledge of whom they are entrusting their care to.”

The Humes said there was public interest in naming Jones, and her not seeking to appeal against the coroner’s ruling could be a sign she was taking responsibility for her role in what happened - which they said wasn’t minor.

They said: “This not a vendetta against a particular staff member. This is about wanting embedded change in the attitudes of staff and management within the mental health service.”

The Crown and Rotorua Trust have received about 1c in the dollar back from more than $10 million in loans to iconic Rotorua business QE Health, which is in liquidation.

The liquidator has also confirmed the company no longer has the $19m purpose-built facility those loans helped pay for.

QE Health, which provided various health and wellness services, went into liquidation late last year, ending a more than 80-year history in Rotorua.

The second liquidator’s report, released in June, said secured claims of $8.04m from Crown Regional Holdings and $2.01m from Rotorua Trust were received.

The entities loaned QE Health money towards its move from its original Whakaue St site to a 3000sq m new facility on Hinemaru St, completed in 2023.

The report showed each entity had been paid $56,734 in the liquidation process, representing 1.13 cents on the dollar for their claims.

Claims totalling $253,801 from former QE Health employees were fully paid out.

No payments had been made for secured claims of $218,499, preferential claims of $347,580 from Inland Revenue and unsecured claims of $1.5m.

QE Health was placed into voluntary liquidation in November and, after failing to secure a buyer, closed in December.

It was originally established in 1942 as a temporary hospital to rehabilitate soldiers returning from World War II. It opened to the wider public in 1948.

Clinical services included rheumatology, physiotherapy, psychology, orthotics, dietetics, and occupational therapy.

The first liquidator’s report in November showed QE Health owed at least $13m to 132 creditors.

It said the company reported it had been unable to generate enough income to cover its costs.

The second liquidator’s report showed the company had an “estimated realisable value” of assets worth $760,227 as of June 2. This included cash, debtors, and plants and equipment.

It owed $10.1m to preferential and secured creditors. The total owed to unsecured creditors was to be determined.

The liquidator would continue working through QE Health’s assets and investigating its records and books.

QE Health had funding from loans and grants for its new build.

These included an $8m loan and a $1.5m grant from the Provincial Growth Fund, a $2m loan and a $1m grant from Rotorua Trust, and a $1m grant from the Rotorua Lakes Council.

The Provincial Growth Fund is now administered by Kānoa, the Government’s regional economic development and investment unit.

Kānoa general manager of investment management Brent Chalmers told the Rotorua Daily Post it was waiting on the liquidator to finalise its work, “so we have a full understanding of the position”.

Chalmers said usual practice would be to write off any unrecoverable funds.

Rotorua Trust chief executive Blair Gilbert said the trust was “deeply disappointed” by the loss of QE Health services, which had benefited people from Rotorua and beyond for decades.

He said the trust had worked closely with the liquidator to recover all available funds and to ensure staff were prioritised for payment.

“Despite the financial loss, Rotorua Trust acknowledges the positive impact generated through its investment during the period QE Health remained operational.”

This included removing the ageing buildings and providing health services for patients, he said.

Gilbert said the trust’s diversified investment portfolio had helped mitigate the overall financial impact.

“We remain focused on achieving strong investment performance to ensure we can continue delivering lasting benefits to the Rotorua community.”

Liquidator Steven Khov told the Rotorua Daily Post the QE Health building was no longer an asset of the company, and it had been passed to the landlord as per its lease agreement.

Khov said he was uncertain if there would be other potential avenues for distributions as the liquidation process remained ongoing.

Landowner Pukeroa Oruawhata Trust chief executive Mark Gibb said its subsidiary, Pukeroa Lakefront Holdings Ltd (PLHL), had reached an agreement with the liquidators to surrender the existing ground lease, with the building reverting to PLHL as the landowner.

PLHL also agreed to buy equipment inside the building following QE Health’s closure.

Gibb said PLHL was saddened by the developments with QE Health and its subsequent closure.

He said PLHL took possession of the building from the liquidator late last year and was exploring potential lease options for the site.

The former interim chief executive of QE Health previously said the primary reason for closure was Health NZ’s “lack of meaningful increases” since 2018 to contract funding, making it “impossible” to cover operating costs.

A potential sale of the business collapsed after Health NZ refused to transfer its contracts, which represented 80% of the business’s income.

Health NZ has said it does not believe its contracting decisions caused QE Health’s closure, and that it understood the decision to place QE Health into liquidation was not based on whether service contracts would transfer.

Patient services formerly provided by QE Health were now being delivered by Health NZ teams and contractors.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Former Tall Blacks coach Tab Baldwin has been permanently banned from university sport in the Philippines, following the deaths of two players at a training boot camp.

In June, the American-Kiwi coach resigned after two athletes he coached at a Manila University drowned.

Strong waves had swept several players from the Ateneo Blue Eagles basketball team into deeper water, the university said. Two players, Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili, lost their lives.

Baldwin was stood down while the university and government agencies investigated the incident in Dipaculao, northeast Philippines. He subsequently announced he would leave his position.

On August 7, the University Athletic Association of the Philippines confirmed Baldwin had been “perpetually banned” from university sport.

A statement from the organisation said: “Thomas Anthony Baldwin is perpetually banned from all UAAP competitions and related activities, in any coaching, administrative, advisory, or official capacity, and he is also prohibited from entering any UAAP competition venue.

“This sanction is final and shall not be appealable.”

Team manager Epok Quimpo, assistant coaches Dean Castaño, Sandro Soriano, Reynaldo Jacinto Jr, Hernan Domingo, Caesar Elumba, Grant Dearns and physical therapist John Rueca were all given indefinite suspensions.

In July, Filipino state media reported charges of homicide and reckless imprudence resulting in homicide had been recommended by justice officials against Baldwin and Dearns, the former Moana Pasifika strength-and-conditioning coach who was also at the Blue Eagles.

Under-pressure hospital EDs show need for healthcare changes – Editorial

New Zealand Herald August 15, 2026

Stories about hospitals suggest there is a critical shortage of emergency department nurses, doctors and beds. And patients are the ones who suffer. Photo / 123rf

It’s an emergency

The stories, like the patients on gurneys in hospital emergency departments, keep coming.

The remedy, conspicuous by its absence.

In January this year, it was reported that Wellington Hospital’s Emergency Department recorded a code red and went into its most critical status – when demand outstrips staff and beds – nearly twice a day in 2025. More than 3200 patients, about 10 a day, had left the ED without being seen.

A Health New Zealand spokesperson described it at the time as a “high dynamic environment”, which is a sanitised representation of a grim reality: there is a critical shortage of ED nurses, doctors and beds. And patients are the ones who suffer.

In Waikato Hospital in late June, a man died after waiting nine hours in pain and a witness in ED later reported that the “staff were set up to fail”.

The New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) provided data that Waikato Hospital’s ED had been under pressure for some time.

Last week, some Auckland patients were being diverted to Whangārei Hospital because of high demand at North Shore Hospital. Whangārei’s emergency department was not having a cup of tea and a lie-down. It was also extremely busy.

According to Health Minister Simeon Brown, the numbers are fine. Brown, however, does not appear to be across the numbers. Last week, he told journalist Jack Tame that since the coalition came into power, the total number of nurses working fulltime had increased by 2100. The actual data showed the fulltime equivalent (FTE) had risen by 54 over two years. Larger figures related to the rise initiated by the previous Labour Government.

Brown has also suggested using AI in hospital administration to alleviate pressure.

This week the Government announced a deal with private hospitals. A kind of health upgrade from cattle class to premium for orthopaedic surgeries.

Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora is spending $300 million on its first long-term contracts with private hospitals to treat backlogs of orthopaedic patients waiting for surgeries in the public health system. That means hip and knee replacements for about 3200 patients a year, for six years.

While no doubt helpful to those waiting, this is not a long-term solution. It does not fix what is arguably a health model in dire need of a rethink. It does not help healthcare workers struggling with staffing and care resources. It does not help a patient in ED who has been waiting for eight hours with a broken elbow, or an anxious parent with an unwell baby.

New Zealand’s health system is a paradox: we pride ourselves on scientific innovation and research, on free public healthcare. And yet our EDs are groaning with the waiting wounded. They are not statistics – they are human beings. A dysfunctional system also harms those who are most vulnerable economically, while also underlining inequities.

Healthcare is now a business. Once upon a time, the 1930s, there were laws codifying free public healthcare administered by Area Health Boards. Along came Rogernomics in the 1980s, and the health system would now follow “free market” principles.

Decades later, Health NZ Te Whatu Ora is defined as having a “strategically aligned entity performance framework”.

Health workers suffering burnout must turn from their patients – “clients” – and those lined up in EDs, and on beds in hospital corridors around the country, and make business cases for resources.

Aotearoa New Zealand’s health system should not be buffeted by the prevailing wind, or a tempest of policies and ideologies of incoming and outgoing Governments.

There is only one moral and economic solution, and that is a system that is politically “untouchable”. One funded and supported by principles agreed by a non-partisan, cross-party framework that serves New Zealanders.

Anything else is a Band-Aid.

A Mount Maunganui business owner has “pulled the plug” on his pizzeria after a fresh Mauao slip caused another road closure and restricted customer access.

Adams Ave, between Pilot Bay and the Maunganui Rd roundabout, has been temporarily closed since July 24 after renewed movement at the site of January’s fatal landslide.

Rustica pizzeria is opposite Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park and the Mount Hot Pools, where six campers died in a landslide on January 22.

The Tauranga City Council estimated 8000 cubic metres of earth shifted in July’s slip. The January landslide involved about 12,000cu m.

News of the slips came after an earthquake struck south of Taumarunui on July 25.

The council is adding rock-filled bags outside shipping containers at the campground as a protective measure.

It aims to reopen Adams Ave and the Pilot Bay boat ramp before the end of this month.

But Rustica owner Michele Delaini said a closed road meant a closed business.

“It’s [the pizzeria] closed indefinitely until we see that there’s going to be a serious improvement from the area.”

Delaini said his business relied on people visiting Mauao.

“We are a takeaway shop, and we rely on Uber. People come here, park, take the pizza and go.

“Since the mountain is closed, and the hot pools are closed, we had to reduce our working hours.”

He said the pizzeria had lost thousands of dollars each month since the landslide.

“We have to pull the plug.”

“If it [the pizzeria] was closed, we only pay the rent. If it is open, we have to pay the staff, we have to pay the food wastage, we have to pay electricity expenses. Everything goes up.”

Delaini said customers, before the landslide, would come for a walk on Mauao, then buy dinner.

“For us, there is no reason to be here.”

He had tried selling but he said nobody wanted to buy a business opposite Mauao while the facilities at its base were closed.

Delaini owned another pizzeria, Basilico, in Pāpāmoa.

Other businesses affected by the Adams Ave closure included Hot Spot Superette, where owner Saed Rajput said the road closure prevented customer access.

“If people wanted to come here, they won’t come; the road is closed.”

He said he was paying his business expenses from his own pocket.

“The water is above my head now.”

Rajput said sales were 90% down.

He no longer had staff. Only he worked at the store.

“I can’t keep the staff to run the business because I haven’t been making money.”

Rajput said businesses needed a timeframe for reopening.

“But there’s no news on when they’re going to open [the mountain] .”

He said a timeframe would provide reassurance that customers would return.

“People will come back to the mountain, they will go for a walk and go to the hot pools; then I’ll start to make money.”

Tauranga City Council recovery manager Charlie Rahiri said rock-filled bags were identified as the preferred solution for shoring up slopes at the campground.

About 900 bags weighing about one tonne each would be used.

An earth bund was previously considered as a replacement for the shipping containers.

However, Rahiri said conditions had changed.

He said the rock-filled bags could be installed quickly and enable the road to reopen.

“The placement of the bags should remove the need for ongoing closures of Adams Ave when level three Trigger Alert Response Plan (Tarp) conditions are met.”

Tarp is a plan developed by geotechnical engineers for monitoring land movement and rainfall on Mauao.

It has three levels of risk and responses to each. Level three actions include evacuating and closing Adams Ave.

Rahiri said the estimated cost was about $120,000 and parts of the construction could be reused in future site work.

He said the campground had not been repaired because it was still unstable.

“In essence, we don’t think it has finished [slipping].”

But works on the base track Te Ara Tūtanga were “progressing well”.

There are 42 slips on Mauao. A slip on the southern face of the Motukauri summit (4WD) track was repaired in June.

“We’re still aiming for a summer reopening,” Rahiri said.

He understood business owners’ frustrations and the impact Mauao’s closure had on them.

“We acknowledge many Mount businesses are experiencing significant financial pressure.

“Council cannot replace lost revenue, but we understand certainty and reopening is the biggest support we can provide, so we are actively prioritising working towards this.”

The council’s external review into the Mauao landslide is due by August 21.

The Government’s inquiry has started and recently welcomed public submissions.

Its final report is expected by December 3.

WorkSafe, police and the coroner are also investigating.

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Air is coming out of the housing bubble. Is now the time for first home buyers?

Sydney Morning Herald August 16, 2026

The housing market in Australia has been a parlour game for the past 30 years, and one that the May budget is now upending.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

James Rosling felt relief rather than excitement when, after a near-three-year search, he bought his first home in early August.

The 33-year-old software engineer said he was lucky to have signed the contract for a $635,000 property in the northern Melbourne suburb of Northcote.

“I think naively I thought that it would be a lot easier than it was,” he said. “But I certainly found it really difficult to find somewhere that I thought would be a good place to live at the price point that I was looking at.”

Rosling had a few requirements for his first foray into a national property market that, by most measures, is the second most expensive in the world. He wanted to avoid a place that had a laundry in the bathroom, a small living space or bedroom, or faced west and got too hot in the afternoon.

That ruled out most properties in his price range, which started at $550,000 and grew to $750,000 over time. And, while fewer homes had been on the market since the May federal budget, he still faced stiff competition from couples and downsizers.

But Rosling is hopeful the budget’s changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax concession will make it easier for other first home buyers to get into the market.

“It’s a positive that the changes the government has made have disincentivised investors. I think that housing is a human right, and I think it’s been a huge failure in government that we have commodified our housing market,” he said. “In the long run [the changes] will probably have a positive impact. But at the moment, I don’t think it has quite yet.”

Rosling, by finally buying a home, has jumped into an extraordinarily Australian parlour game that’s been going on for the past 30 years; one the May budget is now upending.

Five capital cities – Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth – are among the 25 most expensive in the world. Canberra would be on that list if the city were a little larger.

Housing filters into every nook and cranny, from declining home-ownership rates among people in their 20s, 30s and 40s, its impact on everything from fertility rates to job mobility, the surge in the size of mortgages needed to buy into the market to the unusually large proportion of Australians who are landlords.

Less than a third of Americans’ total household wealth is in property. In this country, it’s closer to two-thirds.

So ingrained is the property market in the nation’s psyche that auction clearance rates are now reported like football games. This week, attention turned to another match: financial updates from the nation’s four biggest banks.

The largest home lender of them all, the Commonwealth Bank, this week reported a 15 per cent drop in loan applications since the budget, led by a 28 per cent plunge in applications from investors.

Westpac revealed investor mortgage applications had fallen almost 30 per cent since the May budget. NAB reported a 15 per cent slide in mortgage applications and the ANZ a 12 per cent dip.

While a fall in loans had been expected ever since the Reserve Bank started lifting interest rates earlier this year, in a deliberate effort to slow the economy, the size of the declines was surprising.

It reinforced the turmoil across the entire property market. Dwelling values, as measured by Cotality, have fallen by 2 per cent nationally since their peak in March.

ANZ’s economics team believes prices in Sydney could slip by 14.5 per cent by the end of next year, with Melbourne not far behind with a 12.8 per cent drop before a modest recovery in 2028.

Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn said that applications had stabilised in recent weeks, emphasising the slowdown had followed very strong growth in lending last year.

He paints a glass half-full view of the property market.

Comyn was asked by this masthead if now looked like a “buying opportunity” if he hypothetically had a child of first-home-buying age.

He indicated he would “certainly be looking”. Demand for property had softened but “there’s actually not a huge amount of supply that’s come onto the market”.

“I would think over the next 12 months is not a bad time to be looking at purchasing a home,” Comyn said.

However, Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller told this masthead that mortgage applications from first home buyers had dropped by 32 per cent, more steeply those from investors. He said three increases in official interest rates, the general lift in the cost of living and the government’s budget changes had added to the uncertainty felt by first home buyers looking to make a substantial investment.

“I think first home buyers looking at the market are saying ‘should I buy, is it the right time to buy when it might be a little cheaper in six months?’,” he said. “That has to be having some impact on people.”

Miller is comfortable with what’s occurring currently across the property market, dismissing some suggestions the country is heading for a “collapse”.

Reserve Bank data released this week didn’t aid the cause of those looking to catastrophise what’s occurring.

Despite the pain caused by higher interest rates, borrowers are still well ahead on their repayments.

The repayment buffer among the bottom quarter of borrowers – those most likely to be first home buyers – is more than 10 months. Before COVID, this group were about eight months in front.

The most indebted, and the ones who’ve experienced the biggest fall in the value of their home, are about 20 months ahead.

Miller’s biggest concern is the nation’s long-running failure to build affordable housing.

The country had to find a way to build more homes at lower costs, adding that it was an issue all levels of government, the building industry, unions and even banks had to confront.

“I think there’s definitely more we have to do to build more houses at the right price point,” he said.

News about auction rates and mortgage applications overshadowed a development that normally is central to the housing debate in this country – interest rate settings by the Reserve Bank.

On Tuesday, it held the cash rate steady for a second successive meeting. Although the bank’s economic forecasts suggest rates won’t climb any further, governor Michele Bullock made clear further pain may have to be inflicted on borrowers if inflation fails to ease as expected.

But the governor was particularly keen to also address the growing “negative equity is going to consume us all” bandwagon.

Asked about financial stability, Bullock went out of her way to assuage concerns and commentary that every home buyer was underwater on their loan.

“Housing prices have risen a lot. If you look at the percentage of households who are in negative equity, it’s under 1 per cent,” she said.

“If property prices, I think we’ve done some scenarios, if property prices fell by 20 per cent still only about 5 per cent of households would be in negative equity.”

While the bank does not target house prices, it keeps an eagle eye on how the property market is performing and the effect interest rates have on it.

As Reserve Bank assistant governor Christopher Kent noted on Thursday, falling house values – all things being equal – reduces the pressure to lift interest rates.

The combination of previous rate hikes, the four-year run-up in house prices and the government’s tax changes was all slowing the market.

“All else equal, these changes will tend to reduce the extent to which monetary policy needs to constrain the growth in aggregate demand to help bring inflation back to the RBA’s target,” he told a conference in Sydney.

Numbers released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Friday provided some insight into how the budget’s tax changes – many of which are yet to start – are already affecting the market.

Loans taken out by investors tumbled by 8.6 per cent. Among loans taken out by investors on existing homes, the drop was much larger – almost 15 per cent – but offset by an increase in loans for the construction of new homes.

Independent economist Saul Eslake, a supporter of the government’s changes to property taxation, said the whole point of the changes was to depress demand from investors for existing properties.

“Frankly, I think that’s the point of the measures, although the government seems curiously reluctant to acknowledge and embrace that,” he said.

“If you think, as I do, that the fact that housing has become increasingly unaffordable for a growing share of the population is a problem, then surely things that result in housing becoming cheaper should be welcomed.”

All of this is playing out as potential buyers look for a home.

Toby Raban, 33, who works in digital media and is renting, says the tax changes have had a mixed effect on his search for his first property in North Bondi.

“The market has dipped because of the tax changes, but it’s an enticing time to buy, and I’m confident that a suburb like Bondi ... will bounce back,” he says.

The aspiring rent-vester says he will personally continue renting because he enjoys the flexibility of being able to move suburbs, but that he is keen to find a two-bedroom apartment he can rent out.

Raban says the tax changes have limited his options because they prevent him from negatively gearing the property, which would not be a new build.

“I might move into it one day, but I’m looking to buy it as a long-term investment,” he says.

The Australian housing parlour game could be upended yet again.

Are the parents all right? Why raising children feels harder than ever

Sydney Morning Herald August 16, 2026

In the first part of a new series on modern parenting, we look at why mums and dads are in such a state of distress, and how being “good enough” actually really is enough.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

She is the daughter of a family therapist and has a social work degree but, still, parenting in 2026 is so complex that Genevieve Muir likens it to “learning an entirely new language” to the one known to previous generations.

Thirty years on from when a Californian sociology professor coined “intensive parenting” for the engagement-heavy style that became the benchmark for western child-rearing, parent educator Muir sees people struggling – sometimes “sinking”. The mother of four is frank about her early battle not to lose it herself.

Muir has worked with 40,000 parents and thought hard on the question, “is parenting more personally demanding now (in well-off countries) than in the past, or does it just feel that way?”

“It’s my favourite subject,” says Muir, whose sons are aged 9, 12, 15 and 17.

Western parents – often influenced by “child-centred, expert-guided, emotionally absorbing, labour and financially expensive” intensive parenting – certainly think it is tougher. This is reflected in Pew Research Centre data showing 70 per cent believe it is harder than two or three decades ago.

Fears for their kids’ mental health topped the list of parents’ worries in that 2023 study, but by the middle of this year, both the American chief medical officer and the Australian Parenting Research Centre (PRC) had issued warnings about parents’ own perilous psychological state.

In May, Australia’s largest study of parents and carers, the PRC’s Parenting Today, found almost 60 per cent of the 10,000 surveyed were in moderate or high level psychological distress, struggling with loneliness, self-doubt and lack of self-compassion.

The Victorian government and Minderoo Foundation-funded research found 57 per cent of parents feel lonely as carers, 43 per cent feel guilty, and 47 per cent think they are not doing as well as they should be. A staggering 53 per cent “could not forgive themselves for their parenting mistakes”.

Parental wellbeing declined steadily over the past decade, 66 per cent feel sleep-deprived, and nearly half have persistent self-doubt.

Dr Vivek Murthy, the US Surgeon General, warned two years ago that chronic parental stress had become “a critical public health issue”, blaming “new stressors that previous generations didn’t have to consider”.

Muir sees societal changes and the shift towards engagement-heavy parenting in which the stakes feel high as two drivers of the quiet desperation. Work-life has changed, a sense of village has declined, and economic pressure has ramped up so much that two incomes are often vital.

“We have new knowledge about what kids need, so on top of work we’re intensively parenting,” says Muir. “Now, most people only have one or two kids, and we really put a lot of hope into how they will turn out; there is more fear and more comparison.”

Feeling they need to “optimise” all aspects of childhood, rather than just rearing children like parents of the past, has seriously upped the psychological stress.

Information overload – seeing endless content about concepts once confined to clinicians or academics, such as attachment theory, neurological or behavioral science, and child psychology – adds to confusion and self-doubt.

This is supported by Daniela McCann, director at the Australian Psychological Association who says the fast-moving stream of expert advice, information, social comparison and messaging about optimising child development can be overwhelming.

“While that greater knowledge can be really beneficial, the downside is it creates pressure and anxiety; thinking that the standards of good parenting are exceptionally high and mistakes have long-term consequences.”

Technology’s intrusion into the way day-to-day life runs for both parents and kids puts pressure on parents psychologically because it promotes negative feelings about their performance, says child health specialist and parenting expert Dr Kaylene Henderson.

“For the first time, a generation of parents is expected to be connected to workplaces even when they’re at home, and that means mental presence for children isn’t always possible,” she says. “That very much contributes to parental guilt.”

The “guilt and shame” that Murthy says is pervasive among parents he has met across America got a big mention in his health advisory.

Henderson says parents feel they need to be so vigilant in part because of the loss of a sense of safety and community they grew up with. They sense their kids need far more supervision than they had, and this at a time when more couple families have both parents working full-time even from early on.

“Parents are definitely more stressed, and more anxious,” Henderson says, and children “definitely seem less resilient, and less capable than they once might have been – we are stuck in a very well-intentioned vicious cycle”.

“Everyone is trying to do their best, but the load feels much heavier,” says the mother of two girls and a boy aged 18, 16 and 14 respectively.

McCann, a pyschologist, agrees, saying parenting has “broadened” for this generation and, while her own parents would have considered something like being bullied at school to be primarily the child’s problem to navigate, now “parents are expected to be caregivers, educators, digital safety monitors, emotion coaches and advocates for all things.”

As well as being more hands-off, past parents had little access to anxiety-inducing information about the minutiae of children’s day-to-day lives. “That expansion to the parenting role has really made it not just feel more complex and emotionally demanding, it actually is [more so] than it was for families of a generation or two ago,” McCann says.

Because schools are aware that more children are anxious, they are adding more communication to the already vastly increased amount sent home in the past. Henderson describes it as “schools calling out louder to parents through their inbox”, even though the attention of many parents is maxed out.

Her reassuring mantra is that simply focusing on the foundational relationship parents have with their children supports both to thrive, and that relationship guides the majority of long-term outcomes parents all hope for.

“We’re the first generation of parents who’ve had access to research that can guide the way we interact with our children, which is positive, but that’s not what’s getting out there – it’s [content by] people with a marketing budget,” says Henderson.

She entered the parent education scene because she felt some information being pitched at parents was setting them up to fail, and “that felt unfair and cruel”.

The extent of distress some are feeling as they struggle to meet their own high standards surprised Dr Catherine Wade, principal researcher of the Parenting Today study.

She describes it as concerning that 12 per cent were reporting such high levels of psychological distress that they should be receiving professional support for anxiety or depression, and almost half said they had moderate distress.

This shocked Wade because it shows parents experience higher levels of distress than Australian adults generally. “There must be reasons why parents these days are, in a sociological sense, feeling more under pressure. We’re putting a lot more on ourselves to be perfect,” she says.

“We’re not forgiving ourselves when we make mistakes, the village is definitely shrinking – the supports around parents, that close sense of neighbourhood. We’re definitely seeing a shift in how connected people feel to each other.”

The study found feeling lonely as a parent at least sometimes was consistent across family types (single/partnered) and locations.

“It’s not just single parents, not just mums, or parents with children with complex needs or a disability, or regional parents; it’s pretty universal,” Wade says. “All types of parents are feeling that subjective feeling of loneliness; they might have lots of people around, but they’re feeling lonely in the role.”

On the upside, she says, “these are things we can do something about”.

The irony is that while parents often put their own wellbeing last, according to several of the experts, their welfare is pivotal to the wellbeing of their children. Psychologist and former National Children’s Commissioner, Anne Hollonds, says a debilitating lack of time underlies the increase in parental stress.

“They need you when they are little, and also when they are bigger, but in different ways. We worry a lot about older kids and we are not there with them so much of the time. But as parents we carry the concerns with us,” she says.

The time drought feels constant to parents across the whole of childhood, Hollonds says, and while it is acutely apparent when children are little and need more care, as they become teens the worry about being there can be greater.

Hollonds would like more emphasis put on supporting parents, especially with mental health concerns, in the interests of families. She was surprised as commissioner to hear how often children among the 1500 she spoke with mentioned concerns for their parents’ mental wellbeing.

“We also know the wellbeing of parents is probably one of the biggest factors that affects the wellbeing of children,” she says. “So that’s why we should be worried if there are more issues for parents – more stress and mental health issues, and lack of access to help.”

The good news, and the happy ending to this catalogue of what is putting parents on edge, is that all the experts agree, while perfect parenting is not a healthy goal, “good enough” is both more manageable and better for both parents and children.

Dr Alice Dwyer, consultant psychiatrist and medical director of Parent-Infant and Early Childhood Mental Health at Tresillian early parenting service, says the key concept of the “good enough” parent has been lost as social media projects the idea that constant physical presence with young children, for example, makes for best-practice parenting.

Even babies naturally turn away from parents for a break from the intensity, she says.

Developmental frameworks such as attachment theory have been “social media-fied” and even caricatured, making parents feel they should meet impossible standards of constant availability, but the truth is that more is not necessarily better.

“The perception of what is good enough isn’t widely understood,” says Dwyer. “It comes as a great relief to many parents. The next part is that trying to be perfect could even be a risk for your child.

“So if you really want your child to be secure, we need to take those expectations down a notch – and they will learn that being human is acceptable.”

He’s TV Mr Nice Guy, but Nathan Fillion’s ‘unlikeable’ superhero could be his greatest hit

Sydney Morning Herald August 16, 2026

The Rookie star dials up the charm and makes his tough-talking Green Lantern the hero we need in 2026.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When comic books first carved gods and monsters from cheap newsprint paper, they transformed low-quality wood pulp into invincible icons such as Superman and Batman and the terrifying villains they face. These heroic figures, like their stablemates the Flash and Aquaman, were variously otherworldly princes, noble avengers or scientific geniuses.

Guy Gardner – better known as Green Lantern – had a far more earthly origin story. His childhood was brutal, at the hands of an alcoholic father. He grew up in the shadow of a more popular older brother. And his football career was derailed by injury. Created in print in the late 1960s as an aggressive hothead, he offers a uniquely offbeat take on what it means to be a superhero in 2026.

“Audiences are more intelligent now,” says Nathan Fillion, who plays Gardner’s Green Lantern in the Superman movie series and now in the HBO Max series Lanterns. “When I started reading comic books, they were terrible. They were a drawing of a hero describing action and story, and telling you what’s happening, rather than showing you. Then, comic book stories and art started getting beautiful.

“Much in the same way, I think Batman was darn near happy when he was invented, but now the twist is, what if that guy’s not all just together there, [what if he’s] psychotic? That’s the reality of it. We lean into that kind of stuff, and that’s very satisfying because it allows us to think we could believe in these people.

“Guy Gardner is less complicated. I think he’s overly simplified. He has a sense of right and wrong, of good and evil. I just think if you were around Guy Gardner, you would wish he were a little smarter.”

Guy Gardner was created by John Broome and Gil Kane, first appearing in Green Lantern #59, published in March 1968. Abin Sur, one of the Green Lantern Corps – a kind of space police – crashes on earth and, dying, uses his power ring to find a successor. Eventually, he ends up with three: the more classically heroic Hal Jordan, the more strategic John Stewart, and the abrasive Guy Gardner.

Fillion, revered by genre fans for his early role as Mal Reynolds in the critically revered science-fiction series Firefly, is almost cast against type as Gardner. Elsewhere – for eight years as Richard Castle on Castle, and for eight years and counting as John Nolan on The Rookie – Fillion’s characters have been smart outsiders who came to their power quietly, almost as underdogs.

Castle was a civilian mystery novelist who shadowed police officers, while Nolan is a mature-age police department rookie starting – at least back in season one – a new career after leaving construction. Both use their perspective as outsiders in a tight space where their inexperience is viewed with scepticism as a tool for problem-solving.

And both have a screen life measured in hours: 173 episodes of Castle, between 2009 and 2016, and 144 episodes of The Rookie, between 2018 and now.

Gardner, in striking contrast, has a screen life still measured in minutes. In the 2025 film Superman, he was part of the still-unformed Justice League ensemble, he appeared in the spin-off series Peacemaker, and he will return, in 2027, in the new Superman film Man of Tomorrow.

Lanterns, an eight-episode series commissioned for the streaming service HBO Max, will develop Gardner’s story substantially. In it, he joins the two other Green Lanterns – Hal Jordan, played by Kyle Chandler, and John Stewart, played by Aaron Pierre. And in a substantial nod to the character’s comic book origin story, the series will feature the Green Lantern Corps nemesis, Thaal Sinestro, played by Ulrich Thomsen.

The journey from a life measured in minutes of screen time to hours will be illuminating, Fillion says, though perhaps not in the obvious way. “What I try to strive for is not to change, [it] is for consistency,” he says.

“Because in the Superman film we’re introduced to Guy Gardner, and he has a very specific tone, but Lanterns is a very, very different tone. I thought it would be important that these two worlds exist, but this character exists as well. So I think he had to have some consistency throughout.

“Time spent with a character is time spent witnessing their choices and being there on that journey with them. Our choices, our experiences shape who we are. So longevity inevitably leads to evolution, and taking that journey with a character is, I think, extremely satisfying for an audience member. It’s an investment.”

Why an actor suits a role often lacks rhyme or reason. Chemistry plays a bit part of it – with co-stars, but also between actor and character. In Fillion’s case, Gardner’s dry, dislikeability is tempered by Fillion’s natural charm.

“I have been very fortunate that I have been able to play characters that are extremely likable, and that comes along with a real education as to [why],” he says. “You can’t like a perfect character. Perfect characters don’t exist. You like people because they’re flawed like you and me. You like people because you get them, you can relate to them. On some level, when they fail, you say, I get it because I also have been kicked by life.

“So, there is likeability in being flawed. When it comes to someone like Guy Gardner, who is supposed to be essentially unlikeable, he doesn’t contain malice, he’s just cranky and difficult to be around. We all have someone like that in the family, someone you don’t want to sit next to at Thanksgiving dinner. We’ve all got that person. So, the secret is just playing that guy. Yeah, we get it, but he’s my uncle, so he’s family. He’s that guy.”

Fillion comes to this iteration of the DC Universe with an unusual, even immersive pedigree. He voiced another Lantern – Hal Jordan – in six animated films. But his relationship with the DC Universe goes back to his childhood, he says.

“My parents were high school English teachers, and they encouraged reading, they didn’t care what we read,” Fillion says. “So my choice was comic books. I wasn’t a collector in the beginning as far as following a series because we bought all our comic books second-hand [from the Wee Book Inn in Edmonton, Alberta], so my tastes were extremely varied.”

He knew Guy Gardner’s Green Lantern he says, but – and here’s the twist in the tale – he didn’t like him. “I didn’t see his worth back then, and I didn’t know how beloved he was until I actually got this role and people started talking about Guy Gardner in a way I’d never heard,” Fillion says

At the centre of the Green Lantern canon sits the green power ring each of them wears. In technical terms, it can do almost anything: project a force field, create tools, weapons or vehicles, translate languages and, when needed, let a Green Lantern take flight.

Lifestyle Editor

And it is recharged by reciting the Lantern Corps oath: “In brightest day, in blackest night / No evil shall escape my sight / Let those who worship evil’s might / Beware my power... Green Lantern’s light.”

As a prop on the set of a television series, it does possess talismanic properties, Fillion agrees. That puts it, in pop-cultural terms, alongside a lightsaber from Star Wars, The Doctor’s sonic screwdriver in Doctor Who, or Wonder Woman’s golden lariat.

“What I have found interesting is, given a prop gun, there are times when you have to imitate the kick of that gun,” Fillion says. “Given a blaster of sorts, you have to imbue the object with an action, the force that it reckons for you. Much the same, I had to concoct, and I think everybody who’s been a Green Lantern has to feel the force of something happening, and create that effort that it comes with this physical effort.

“For me, the ring, as far as what it conjures, I think about the reality of it. If I had a ring like that, I would be charging it every other hour, I would never take it off. And yet, I fidget constantly, so I’d take it off, and I would be so paranoid in those moments. I’d be just furiously worried about it constantly.”

Lanterns streams on HBO Max from August 17.

‘Little by little cities will have to recede’: Coastal flooding is the sleeper climate issue

Sydney Morning Herald August 16, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When Virginia Jones moved to the Tweed Coast with her young family nearly a decade ago, saltwater flooding her home was not the type of sea change she had in mind.

She knew her home at Bogangar near Cabarita Beach was on a floodplain, near the coastal lagoon and creeks, but it was built on piers and had never gone underwater since its construction in the 1970s.

On the last day of February 2022, she went to bed to the drumbeat of heavy rain. She woke to find that one of the family’s two cars was inundated, the other was trapped, and the water was lapping at the bottom rungs of the eight steps to her front door.

The family – two adults, two children then aged nine and 12, and two dogs – evacuated in a neighbour’s kayak.

“The next day when we waded into our street and walked into our house, we realised that [the water] had come about 30 centimetres up the walls,” Jones says.

“At the time, I thought it just meant replacing some furniture and cleaning walls, but in actual fact, when your home floods, you have to rip the plaster off because otherwise mould grows underneath.”

It would be more than a year before the family returned home, and Jones says she and her husband, Tim Lawson, only came back at all because they could do radical flood-proofing.

Since the house was on piers, they decided to raise the entire structure. The front door is now above the flood line – more than twice as high as before, with enough space underneath the house for a full-size netball hoop – and they also added a second storey.

Coastal hazard is a key risk in NSW as sea levels rise and the upstream flooding risk worsens because of extreme rainfall events and urban development – and one that we have barely had to grapple with yet. Up and down the coast, our suburbs and townships are built on low-lying land around coastal lagoons, lakes and estuaries. Lake Illawarra alone – subject to flooding off the escarpment and inundation by the sea – has tens of thousands of people living around its shores. The same is true for Lake Tuggerah and Lake Macquarie, north of Sydney.

In Sydney, the northern beaches, home to about 273,000 people and surrounded on three sides by water, is one of the areas with the highest overall coastal risk both now and in the future. Hundreds of thousands of people also live in low-lying areas around Gamay-Botany Bay and the tidal zone of the Cooks River – and are already grappling with soaring insurance costs.

Coastal hazard is the biggest future risk to the built environment in the state because of sea level rises, according to the NSW State Disaster Mitigation Plan put out in February 2024. This could cause both coastal erosion of sandy beaches and shoreline and either permanent or tidal coastal inundation above the current high-tide mark. About 85 per cent of the state’s population lives within 50 kilometres of the coastline, making the state particularly vulnerable, the plan says.

In 2023, the local government areas with the highest coastal hazard were Shellharbour, Newcastle and Port Stephens but by 2060 this will change to Port Macquarie-Hastings followed by Clarence Valley and Tweed, the mitigation plan says. The LGAs with the greatest overall risk – factoring in the number of exposed properties and assets – were Central Coast, Northern Beaches and Tweed, but this will change to Northern Beaches, Byron and Central Coast.

CSIRO climate economist Russell Wise says there is an urgent need for a conversation about managed retreat from areas at high risk from sea-level rises.

“We’re talking about having to relocate entire communities because we cannot defend our entire coastline,” Wise says. “And we don’t want to defend our entire coastline because we’d lose our beaches and our dunes systems and our coastal ecosystems.”

Under a low-emissions scenario (known as Shared Socioeconomic Pathway1-2.6), sea levels at Port Kembla – as a reference point for the NSW coast – are expected to rise between 23 centimetres and 56 centimetres by 2100, Adapt NSW says. That’s compared with the 1995-2014 baseline.

Under a medium-emissions scenario (SSP2-4.5), which is closest to the current trajectory, it’s 37 centimetres to 73 centimetres by the end of the century. Under a high-emissions scenario (SSP3-7.0), it’s between half a metre and 91 centimetres.

High-profile examples of coastal erosion include Collaroy-Narrabeen on the northern beaches where a 1.3-kilometre hard sea wall was built to protect 49 multimillion-dollar properties built on the sand dunes. Now the same thing will happen at The Entrance North, after the NSW Land and Environment Court overturned the Central Coast Council’s refusal of a permanent 90-metre seawall designed to protect three beachfront apartment blocks.

In Collaroy-Narrabeen, landowners paid 80 per cent of the $25 million construction costs and state and local governments covered the remainder. There is already lobbying for future coastal protection works to be funded the same way.

Taxpayers subsidising a seawall to protect private properties worth millions of dollars is controversial, and quite a different matter to taxpayers funding infrastructure to protect public land and assets. Even if private landowners stumped up for the entire cost, coastal erosion experts say a hard seawall can have detrimental effects on the beach below.

Research from the University of Sydney and the University of Wollongong suggests that beaches with natural dunes would be able to retreat inland, retaining their general shape, while those backed by hard coastal cliffs or seawalls, would have nowhere to go, so the expanse of sand would shrink and eventually drown.

6:39

Adaptation and Australia’s climate crisis

From floods to extreme heat: The human cost of Australia’s changing climate

In NSW, the emergency services levy, which funds fire services and the State Emergency Service, is applied to home insurance, though the state government is reviewing that. Former planning minister Rob Stokes, himself based on the northern beaches, says the levy should be applied to people’s rates so that people are paying for the risks the community bears based on where their properties are.

“It’s a really difficult thing to say and, of course, there have to be equity considerations and all the rest for people who can’t afford to pay, but at the end of the day, if you’re living in an inherently risky location, then that should be reflected in the value of your property,” Stokes says.

“Currently because those recurrent costs are not attached to your property value, you still will find a beachfront in Collaroy, for example, selling for $7 million or $10 million when fundamentally there’s a much higher risk associated with living there than living two streets further back from the beach.”
