2:28

Clean-up begins after Sydney's Northern Beaches inundated with floodwaters

After flash flooding on Sydney’s Northern Beaches saw roads, cars and houses submerged, the damage is being assessed.

But coastal erosion is not the only coastal hazard. There’s also the sleeper issue of coastal inundation – where sea levels rise so that low-lying land is permanently underwater or inundated regularly at high tide.

Coastal flooding occurs more slowly than with rivers and is generally shallower and calmer – making it less dangerous to human life. Yet it is still highly damaging to people’s homes and, rather than an overnight disaster, it is a slow-burn problem affecting millions of NSW residents.

Stokes says coastal and estuarine inundation will affect more properties than coastal erosion. Many relatively affordable postwar homes were located around coastal lagoons because the land was flat and easy to subdivide, he said.

“A lot of the headlines get taken by coastal erosion because it’s so dramatic, but when you look at development around coastal lagoons, and also the relative values of properties around, for example, Woy Woy and Umina, or Lake Illawarra, or Ballina, or any of those coastal lagoons, there are thousands of properties and they might be lower value properties [than beachfront homes], but there’s a lot more of them and a small increase in sea level rise will affect a huge number of people,” Stokes said.

“The good news there is, there are engineered solutions to these problems such as revetment walls, but ... you want to avoid doing that if at all possible because ultimately, you’re fighting against nature rather than working with it.”

Independent MP Zali Steggall, whose federal electorate of Warringah encompasses the northern beaches, has been banging the drum of climate adaptation for some time, and says coastal flooding is one of the issues that need more prominence.

“Coastal flooding as a risk keeps getting underestimated because people think it’s just about sea level rises,” Steggall says. “But the reality is, coastal flooding will occur in many ways and our infrastructure is not equipped to cope.

“For example, we had a rain event with maximum rainfall, maximum precipitation in a period of an hour back in 2022, and it coincided with a high tide event, which meant all of our stormwater infrastructure essentially failed, and we had flooding in vast areas of an urban environment – we had cars floating down streets, schools were closed, we had Manly Corso underwater.”

Steggall says sea level rises do not just affect the coast, but further upstream into estuaries where they affect the tides, river flows and stormwater capacity. She is excited by research into nature-based solutions such as mangroves to deal with floodwaters along an estuary.

This plays into the idea of “sponge cities”, an urban design concept that arose in China and has been influential internationally. Dr Elisa Palazzo, a senior lecturer in urban design and landscape architecture at the University of NSW, says it builds on earlier work that Australia led in “water sensitive urban design” – but like everything to do with China, it’s on a grander scale with more central government control.

Rather than rigid infrastructure such as concrete storm drains, the city design might use porous roads and pavements to allow rainwater to seep into the soil, green roofs to allow vegetation to absorb water, rain gardens and vegetated ditches that filter and slow down run-off, and low-lying parks that become wetlands during severe storms to hold water before releasing it slowly.

However, Palazzo says sponge cities will be more useful for dealing with riverine flooding than coastal flooding.

“With sea level rise, the floods along the coastline will not be preventable,” Palazzo says. “Obviously, we can have mangroves, and we need to recreate that soft edge because even no wall will be enough to retain the force of an ocean. We already know this. But what is going to happen is that little by little cities will have to recede, and that is already happening.”

Palazzo says we will also need to look at architecture that can stand above the water level – architecture on stilts like Jones and Lawson’s home in Cabarita or floating buildings, which are starting to be used in The Netherlands.

Jones refinanced to pay for the rebuild of her home because insurance only covered the cost of replacement, not of improvements to make a home more resilient. Once again, it raises that key question: who pays? Should it be individuals whose homes are vulnerable, or should taxpayers pay? Insurance is not always available or affordable – and it also generally does not cover “acts of the sea”.

The Australian Local Government Association wants the federal government to create a $400 million a year adaptation fund. The Make Big Polluters Pay alliance, backed by some local councils and environmental and social justice organisations such as Greenpeace, Oxfam and the Uniting Church, say that fossil fuel companies should contribute.

CSIRO’s Wise favours some form of land swaps rather than buybacks. So far, he says, governments in both Queensland and NSW have paid the pre-disaster market rate for buybacks, setting an unsustainable precedent.

“We need to reconsider the approach of buying people out,” Wise says. “Instead, we could be saying ‘here’s a place that you can go to’, and it may be way cheaper to do that than actually pay a person out and then expect them to go and find a place in a market where there aren’t any places to go to because of the under supply.

“This would require strategically building places in receiving environments, in more affordable housing that’s actually safer as well, and then give people the option to move to those places.”

He notes that this would take time, so governments would need to manage the risks and impacts in the short term.

The NSW Reconstruction Authority is managing a buyback program in both the Northern Rivers and Central West following the devastating 2022 floods. Planning Minister Paul Scully says he is not aware of the government contemplating any further buybacks, adding that the topic needs to be treated sensitively.

“I’m an economist as well,” Scully says. “And I can appreciate a dispassionate analysis from a CSIRO economist, but they’re also people’s homes, right? People have built their lives in particular areas, and asking people to uproot themselves and move, even if you’re moving in the same area, is a big deal.”

The authority is developing a managed relocation policy to consider issues such as buybacks and land swaps. It is expected to be completed later this year, and included in the next version of the State Disaster Mitigation Plan.

Wise says the burden of coastal inundation is not just about private property, but also falls on local governments trying to provide infrastructure. Already, the costs of maintaining roads at a basic level has gone through the roof for both inland and coastal councils because of flooding and extreme temperatures.

“Sea level rise is a significant chronic risk that will start to really rear its head,” Wise says. “It’s the nuisance effect of continual or periodic inundation or flood events, which aren’t classified as disasters but wear infrastructure down.”

The Reconstruction Authority, which was established in 2022, has been working on more specific regional plans to follow the State Disaster Mitigation Plan. Work is well progressed on a multihazard plan for the Northern Rivers that will take in coastal hazard. The agency also did a pilot study in the Shoalhaven-Illawarra, testing out different methodologies for assessing risk and engaging with communities, but this is not publicly available.

The authority’s acting executive director for disaster risk reduction, Louise Shepherd says the statewide plan makes it clear that floods and coastal hazard are the biggest future risks to the built environment. Her agency has been working carefully through possible responses, she says.“Sea walls of various types, including rock revetments, are big infrastructure, and would need to go through a pretty technical process to see if it’s the right solution in a particular place,” Shepherd says. “Other examples of what we could do to mitigate coastal hazard include beach nourishment and dune planting.”The feasibility and suitability of large-scale offshore sand reserves and other sources for beach nourishment has come under the microscope and this will form part of the Northern Rivers plan and also the updated statewide plan due by the middle of next year.

This work sits alongside the requirement for coastal councils to come up with coastal management plans, which was introduced in 2016 and took effect in 2018 but with no deadline to complete the work. A coastal management plan is a long-term, strategic document, and having a registered plan provides easier planning pathways than development applications and access to funding grants.

The NSW Audit Office reported in September last year that the coastal management framework was “not being effectively implemented” and needed more oversight from the state government. At the time, using figures from April last year, only 16 out of 55 coastal councils had at least one completed plan. More than a year later, it’s crept up to 18. This is despite the state government making 373 grants totalling $73.72 million since 2016 to help councils get the work done.

The government says it has accepted all the recommendations of the auditor-general either fully or in principle. There are now 27 coastal plans covering both open coast and estuarine environments across 55 councils. Some councils have more than one plan, and some plans have more than one council, but 37 councils are yet to complete at least one plan.

NSW Climate Change Minister Penny Sharpe says the issues are “challenging and complex” and both levels of government are working through them.

Residents have had to take matters into their own hands. Back at Cabarita Beach, Jones and Lawson had better options than most of their neighbours, many of whom could not afford to do anything except replace and hope for the best. There were some federal government grants, but eligibility was too limited to be helpful, Jones says.

Her neighbour Bernie Zietlow also renovated to floodproof his home using his insurance payout and favours from his tradie mates.

His house was on the ground rather than piers, so raising it was not an option. Instead, he replaced the ruined carpets and tiles with polished concrete floors throughout most of the house and tiled the bathroom with waterproof materials, like a swimming pool.

The kitchen looks normal but is made out of a PVC material that can survive underwater, and stone tops. The oven is above the microwave because the microwave can be moved, but the oven cannot. All his power points and the air conditioner are now above the flood level.

It took him 12 months, but he says next time the floods come, he’ll be able to hose it out.

Zietlow knows that the coastal flooding will get worse as climate change progresses, but at 67, he thinks he won’t be around to see it. A keen surfer, he loves living near the beach, and assumes his children will bulldoze the home after he’s gone since it only has two bedrooms.

“I’m sure that we’ll get floods again, but I’m not going to worry about them,” Zietlow says. “It didn’t affect me emotionally as much as it did a lot of other people for a number of reasons, No.1 is that I lost a son in 2011, so I had a big, big lesson about what’s important in life. I wasn’t that concerned about losing things because I knew I could replace them.”

Additional reporting: Michael Bachelard and Gay Alcorn

After Killing Heidi, Ella Hooper was at a crossroads. Then a magazine washed up on a beach

Sydney Morning Herald August 16, 2026

Now 43 and after a few years marred by tragedy, the one-time teen rock goddess is back with an entirely new sound.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Reconciling with the past is hard when there are reminders scattered all around you. Nobody knows this better than Australian musician Ella Hooper. To a generation of fans, she will forever be the spirited young girl who rose to fame in the late ’90s as the lead singer of rock band Killing Heidi.

By 2000, at just 17, she’d already made the cover of Rolling Stone Australia. It was an era when bands could get noticed on community radio stations and go on to become certified rock stars. For Killing Heidi, it culminated in their debut album, Reflector, soaring to the top of the ARIA charts.

1:23

Ella Hooper is stepping back into the spotlight

She was the face of Aussie rock at 17. Now 43, the former Killing Heidi singer is getting back to her roots.

That meteoric rise coincided with a legendary spot on the Big Day Out festival line-up, also in 2000, where headliners the Red Hot Chili Peppers famously declared to their sweaty, adoring fans that they wanted to meet Ella Hooper backstage. Little did they know she was in the mosh pit with her friends.

Hooper shot to fame alongside her brother Jesse, two years her senior. That brief period has defined the rest of their lives, and it’s taken Hooper many years to make peace with it. The dreadlocks, bandeau top and tight pants she sported in the early 2000s create less internal cringe these days as she’s learnt to look more kindly on those images of her past.

Now 43, Hooper has traded rock posturing for rootsy Americana and is considering relocating to Nashville to give her boot-scooting passion a rightful crack. “The bombshell is I was never a rocker,” says Hooper, “so returning to country music makes absolute sense. I’ve listened to country since I was about 15.”

Now, following the death of both her parents, Hooper has allowed herself space to grieve and is leaving no stone unturned in a mission to land where she feels most at home.

She has no regrets about the 2000s either. “I absolutely loved being in a rock band. It shaped me, but song-wise it’s never been a genre I gravitate towards. I’m not claiming to be the world’s most authentic Americana singer, but it’s a genre that fits like a glove for me.”

Indeed, it was the songs of American “highway women” such as Linda Ronstadt, Bonnie Raitt, Emmylou Harris and Lucinda Williams that inspired her to sing in the first place.

Born and raised in regional Victoria’s Violet Town, population 950, Hooper went from a quiet country life to stardom rather quickly thanks to a song, Kettle, she wrote in the mid-’90s. It was noticed by Triple J, which in turn led to a major label deal. (Her life at Benalla High School is forever marked by the day she was taking the school bus home when Killing Heidi’s hit song Weir came on the radio, to much applause.)

Her father, Jeremy, loved English literature and listened to Bob Dylan and Neil Young, igniting a love of language. He also owned a huge vinyl collection that laid the foundations of his daughter’s tastes, while mum Helen’s record collection was filled with Buffy Sainte-Marie and Eva Cassidy.

“The music that had the biggest impact on me was American singer-songwriter Iris DeMent,” says Hooper of those formative years. “Every song of hers is etched in my soul. She is the most underrated writer in the world – I put her up there with Bob Dylan.”

But starting Killing Heidi with brother Jesse, and the almost instant stardom that came with it, meant hitting pause on her dream of being a country music artist. “I often really struggled with the fame that came my way,” she admits. “I didn’t even have my periods when the band started. I was literally a child. The music was of its time – a sound that was a cultural moment. It was never meant to be an ongoing legacy, musically speaking, but it became that.”

When Killing Heidi came to an end in 2006, Hooper needed to take a step back. When she released her debut solo album, In Tongues, in 2014, it was the first time she’d written songs without her brother. But it was still essentially a rock record. Hooper’s watershed moment came during a wellness retreat in Lombok with her mother in 2017.

“I was at a point in my career where I wasn’t really doing anything and didn’t have much money,” she says. “I was trying to get into hosting work on radio and TV, but chose the worst back-up career – it was just as dicey. There are a lot of tightly held positions in Australian media and not many openings. I wasn’t exactly having an easy time in my career, but I had this itch to do something.

“Mum and I booked a yoga retreat and did lots of meditation, but while I was walking along the beach, a copy of Rolling Stone magazine washed up. Dubbed the ‘Nashville Special Edition’, it was a real smack-you-in-the-face moment. I grabbed it. The magazine was still readable and I hugged it and thought, ‘Why not? This is what I am meant to be doing.’”

A trip to the US followed, with all highways leading to Nashville. A subsequent performance spot at Americanafest confirmed to Hooper that she was at her happiest among other country music lovers, and she returned to its stages on and off as often as she could until COVID-19 hit.

Then came Hooper’s second solo album, Small Town Temple, written in Violet Town in 2020-21. It featured her parents on some tracks and gave her a chance to push against the grain and settle into the haystack. After its release in 2023, the album was nominated for an Australian Music Prize and also made it to No. 1 on the local country music charts.

Sadly, however, that came after the “worst year” of Hooper’s life; she lost her mother to breast cancer in early January 2022 and her father had died just a couple of weeks earlier. “Losing my parents was hard, is still hard,” she says. “Mum got sick, then Dad got sick.

“I hate to admit it, but I got through it by working non-stop. I am not very good at stopping and feeling all of my emotions. I’m a workaholic. I haven’t gone to drink or drugs, but I went into overdrive with work to keep me on track.”

She also realised it was what she had to do. “If I want this next chapter of my career to work, I have to give it my all. I feel blessed that I had my parents always behind me on this journey.”

Her new album, Overnight Success, made in Nashville last year, features a who’s who of the city’s players, including Sheryl Crow’s drummer Fred Eltringham and Linda Ronstadt’s pedal steel player Dan Dugmore.

“This may sound self-involved or a little callous, but I’ve never actually done what I want to do until now,” she says. “I’ve always taken the long way around to make people feel comfortable, from managers and record companies to, I hate to say it, band and family members. I was always doing what they wanted, and now I am going for it.”

After moving between rentals six times around North Melbourne, she has finally found home in Kensington. Back in Violet Town, the childhood home is up for sale but her bond with brother Jesse remains her anchor. “Jesse is one of my best friends, my rock. We don’t always see eye to eye, but growing up in the country meant we bonded over isolation – we were the last house on a dirt road. Jesse’s a father, a nurturer, and we still have Killing Heidi on the back burner for the occasional trip down memory lane.”

Emerging from a long-term relationship has also spurred a shift in Hooper as she’s come to realise how much she counts on her female friends to help her through hard times. “I didn’t get to university because I was so busy with Killing Heidi, but I am lucky to have this sorority around me. I had a pretty major break-up in the last two years and girlfriends – you need them. I always attribute solid friendships and community to the reason I’m semi-sane on a good day.”

As for the mood of her new single, I Got Eyes (On You), Hooper is definitely heartbroken but walking out with her head high. “I had a bit of a problem with people-pleasing and needing to be liked by everybody for a great chunk of my life,” she reflects. “Writing this album has been a huge relief for me on so many levels. I was always apologising for my success and opportunities and I caught myself being a bit of a shrinker – the sort of person who always said, ‘Oh no, you go first.’ I had a mantra: ‘I couldn’t possibly take another opportunity because I’ve had so many.’

“Then I realised that’s not right either. It’s not about going slower or being smaller to make sure you’re not getting in anyone’s way. It’s about playing your natural game. Anything that doesn’t fit that matrix, I’ve rejigged. And in some cases, relationships have ended.”

Overnight Success is out October 2. Ella Hooper will be touring in October.

Kabul review – this thriller about Afghanistan’s abandonment is every bit as gripping as it is horrifying

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 20:50:06 GMT

This tense, powerful six-parter starkly captures the nation’s slide into oppressive terror. Its capturing of a shameful moment in history is hugely vivid

The final episode of Kabul pointedly soundtracks its opening scene with a speech given by George W Bush when America invaded Afghanistan in 2001. “The oppressed people of Afghanistan will know the generosity of America and our allies,” Bush’s teleprompter tells him to say. “The United States of America is a friend to the Afghan people.”

This taut six-part thriller, a pan-European co-production, is set in Afghanistan’s capital in August 2021, at the end of a 20-year western intervention that has, ultimately, not delivered the stated goal of freeing the country’s people from the fundamentalist authoritarianism of the Taliban regime. To the contrary, the Taliban are ready to install a more fearsome version of their old government as soon as the scheduled withdrawal of the Americans and their European allies takes place.

The series sketches how, for the vast majority of ordinary Afghans, living under oppressive terror is now their only possible future: the foreigners who arrived in the wake of President Bush’s announcement are about to become absent friends, if indeed friends is what they ever were. But for the purposes of the drama, we are with the fortunate few who have a ticket out. Their connection to the visitors from Nato has given them the paperwork necessary to be evacuated to new lives in the west.

Kabul’s first episode starkly captures the slow-dawning realisation, among citizens and the last few diplomats in the French and Italian embassies, that those visas might just be one final batch of broken promises. The Taliban have entered the city and are not sticking to the agreed timetable: a piece of paper will offer no protection from being imprisoned, killed or just physically prevented from accessing the increasingly besieged airport.

The drama uses the old but powerful trick of focusing on a single family, headed by matriarch Zahara (Darina Al Joundi). Her work as a prosecutor has seen her imprison countless Taliban fighters as terrorists, so she will be shot on sight if recognised by the forces storming into Kabul. Her husband Baqir (Vassilis Koukalani) is in the middle of trying to persuade her she should leave everything behind immediately when he is proven right by gunfire on their street. A wrenching, terrifying scene sees Zahara abandon a beloved elderly colleague who isn’t fit enough to dash to the French embassy. Everywhere, impossible decisions are hurriedly being made.

As Zahara and Baqir flee, they are forever on the phone to their adult children, neither of whom can be trusted to prioritise their own safety. We meet Fazal (Shervin Alenabi) as he mans a rural checkpoint on behalf of the Afghan army. Having been forced to abandon it by the Taliban’s overwhelming numbers, instead of heading to the city he moves further out into the country in search of his old CIA handlers; thus becoming our way of seeing the situation in the nation outside Kabul, and assessing the role of the last remaining Americans.

Providing an insight into what dealing with the Taliban close-up is like, meanwhile, is the family’s daughter Amina (Hannah Abdoh), a hospital doctor for whom starting again in Europe holds no appeal. She has trained to help sick and injured Afghans and is determined to keep doing that. But when the Taliban enter the hospital, she (and we) see that their psychopathic aggression and stupid dogma cannot be reasoned with or resisted. One is reminded of Margaret Atwood’s warning that everything in The Handmaid’s Tale has already happened, somewhere.

The Taliban immediately set about building a crude cinder-block wall to split the hospital building in two, enforcing their strict separation of men and women with no regard for patients’ health. On the ward, Amina has bonded with a girl of primary-school age who benefits greatly from the calming distraction of songs on her iPod - until a Taliban soldier charges in and rips the device from the girl’s hands, because “music is haram”.

Will Zahara’s family be reunited, and can the good-hearted westerners – including Giovanni (Gianmarco Saurino), a hesitant, nerdy administrator who suddenly becomes the Italian consul and has to rapidly transform himself into a steely and proactive diplomat – save all the people they promised to protect? The answer to the latter question is a doom-laden no, but as Kabul establishes itself as an efficient, empathic drama, infused with political rage without being slowed down by it, we care about the struggle.

It’s not perfect – it has weaknesses for speechified dialogue, and for characters’ journeys converging in unlikely ways – but its thriller tropes, of a race against time and of risks taken under the gaze of an implacable enemy, are utilised effectively to make the story as compelling as it is appalling. August 2021 in Kabul was an awful, shameful moment in history; this show vividly re-lives it.

Kabul aired on BBC Four and is available on iPlayer in the UK and on SBS On Demand in Australia

Atsuko Okatsuka: ‘Fans have cut their hair to look like mine, which is a huge commitment’

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 20:00:09 GMT

The comedian and actor on her love for White Chicks, getting a bad Yelp review as a dog walker and doing stand-up during an earthquake

You went to film school; what movie do you rewatch or return to most?

This would not be an answer that my film school would respect, or expect: White Chicks by the Wayans brothers. It’s about two brothers who are pretending to be rich white girls from the Hamptons. I love when something’s super stupid and silly, and there’s a scene where this group of [white] girls is in the car singing, and the two brothers have to pretend to know Vanessa Carlton’s A Thousand Miles, and I was like, “Oh my god, I’ve been there!”

I think I was 16 when I watched it for the first time, and I finally knew enough English and also slang, and it also had physical humour, which I grew up watching a lot in Japan. So it was the perfect blend of “Oh, I’m an Asian American now”.

What’s the strangest job you’ve ever had?

I used to walk dogs in LA, and there’s a bad Yelp review about me, saying that I only walked Charlie the terrier mix for 10 minutes instead of the full 30. And I did do that. But it was a rainy day and the dog didn’t want to keep walking, and it was shaking, so I brought it back to the house. But turns out the owner of the dog had a friend spying on me and timing me from the moment I let the dog out and back in. I guess it’s not a weird job, but it’s a memorable one.

What’s the best thing you learned from someone you worked with?

Chelsea Handler is a good friend of mine, and she says about jealousy: just keep in mind that there is room for everyone. You may go, “I wanted first place, like that person”. But you have a role in life in whatever field you’re in. So never compare yourself to others – we’re all made so different.

What’s the most chaotic thing that’s happened to you on stage?

I was doing a stand-up set in Pasadena [California] and a 7.1 magnitude earthquake hit as I was walking on stage. You can see it on YouTube. I was freaked out because I have no skills to help in an earthquake. I went to art school! But I am quick on my feet, I’m funny, and I do care about people. I think having a mom with schizophrenia, and living in the US as an undocumented migrant for seven years – I was like, I can deal with anything. What’s a 7.1 earthquake? This is like the chillest heckler in my life.

When you get to a hotel, what’s the first thing you do?

Every time, I’m genuinely so stoked that I’m not in my house, in my mess. Thank goodness I’m away from my dishes, I’m away from my dirty underwear. I only have clean ones because that’s all I brought.

Is there anything you do to make it feel like home?

Oh no, I never really feel at home anywhere. Even in my own home, sometimes I feel like a stranger. Maybe it’s because I moved around a lot as a kid – I still don’t settle down easily. I’m always like, “Gotta be ready to leave at any point!” Maybe it’s from being undocumented for so long? Or living in a garage for seven years. But I’m always like, we’re gonna get kicked out soon, somehow!

What video is guaranteed to make you laugh?

There’s this video a woman made for her husband, pointing out all the messes he’s made around the house – using a stick with a tiny hand with a pointing index finger. And she does it really aggressively sometimes. It makes me laugh so hard.

What’s been your most memorable interaction with a fan?

A couple of people have cut their hair to look like mine, which is a huge commitment. There was another fan who came to my show wearing a wig of my bowl cut. Her name was Atsuko too. She said, “People used to have a hard time pronouncing my name, and it was always an insecurity of mine – I even wanted to change my name at one point in my life. But because of you, people are able to say my name, and I feel less alone and more seen because of it.” That was cool.

What are you secretly really good at?

I’m really good at physical therapy, especially for senior citizens. Like, if my grandma’s knees are hurting or my mom’s knees are hurting, I know the right exercise to strengthen the muscles around there. I think it’s from my days teaching dance fitness. I got really into fitness in junior high, and studied it a lot on my own – and I was a cheerleader too. So I know how to rehabilitate if someone’s injured.

If you had to appear on a reality TV show, which one would it be?

I want to go on one of the love shows, even though I’m married. Maybe me and my husband could do it. They’ve never had a married couple on Love Island, and they need antagonists, they need villains.

You seem very wholesome; I’m not confident you’d be a great villain …

Well, thank you. I do tend to be positive. But there’s a surprising edge to me. I think people think I’m more wholesome than I am.

If you could plan a fantasy dinner party of people – living or dead, real or fictional – who’s on your list?

Lucille Ball, Stitch [from Lilo and Stitch]. Charlie Chaplin. I want to meet Hachiko, the akita dog that everyone in Japan loves because he loyally waited for his owner at the same train station for years. Maybe Sia, because I’m friends with Kathy Griffin, and she’s really close to her, and so Sia and I see each other sometimes, and I want to invite someone I don’t usually see. And Paddington [Bear].

What a totally normal, natural mix of guests.

I don’t know. I feel like fights will break out. Maybe put Mary, Jesus’s mother, in there too. I have questions.

What would you ask her?

Any regrets?

Atsuko Okatsuka’s The Big Bowl Tour is in Brisbane on 16 August; Adelaide on 18 August; Perth on 19 August; Sydney on 21 August; and Melbourne on 22 and 23 August

Science or fiction? Shadowy ‘paper mills’ let you pay to be a published author – of fraudulent research

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 20:00:07 GMT

Paper mill activity has exploded in recent years, polluting the scientific ecosystem with falsified data and compromising medical research

Dr Reese Richardson’s phone constantly buzzes with notifications. The scientific research integrity specialist has been tracking shadowy organisations known as “paper mills”, which turn a profit by offering fraudulent academic authorship of scientific papers, IP registrations and other scholarly outputs.

For a fee, paper mills offer to list people as authors of scientific journal articles, often of falsified research that bypasses the peer review process.

Richardson has joined dozens of groups across apps such as Telegram, WhatsApp and Facebook where a buffet of fraudulent and fabricated research is advertised to hundreds of members. “I can just look through my notifications and I can see that I’ve gotten, like, 20 WhatsApp messages from paper mills in the last 24 hours,” he says.

Scientists are under constant pressure to publish new research papers which, in many parts of the world, remain the currency of academia. They beget more grant funding and accolades, and enhance academic profiles. But robust, high-quality science takes time, and papers can take years to get published.

Paper mills offer a fraudulent shortcut, using instant messaging and social media platforms to find prospective buyers looking for papers and patents to stack their CVs. According to an analysis Richardson conducted with Anna Abalkina and Spencer Hong, the median price to buy authorship is around US$800 (A$1,150).

In a recent paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed, the trio of scientists led by Richardson, formerly at Northwestern University in the US, detailed more than 18,000 advertisements from seven paper mills across seven countries between 2020 and 2026.

“We wanted to get an idea, across a wide range of paper mills, countries, topics and product types how much these things actually go for,” he says. “What we put together is the largest ever dataset of paper mill advertisements.”

They found many groups advertising authorship of scientific manuscripts across Telegram, Facebook and various websites for as little as US$30.

In the last 15 years, paper mill activity has exploded, with one estimate produced by Richardson in 2025 suggesting their products have been doubling approximately every 18 months. The journal articles produced by these paper mills typically bypass the accepted scientific editorial process of peer review, either because the journals do not institute those processes or because editors are themselves part of paper mill activities.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

This amounts to an industrialised injection of falsified data, polluting the scientific ecosystem and compromising medical research, drug discovery and clinical trials. The scale is massive: in 2023, Hindawi, a now defunct journal brand owned by major publisher Wiley, retracted more than 8,000 articles. A further 3,000 retractions came by the end of 2024.

Richardson says his research is a useful starting point for trying to grapple with how and where paper mills operate, and who they target. The advertisements are like fingerprints at a crime scene, potential evidence of malicious activity. “You can get a lot of information from the advertisements,” he says. He has directly tracked some of these to fraudulent papers in the scientific literature.

Other advertisements relate to copyrights and design registrations, another area ripe for fraud, which may provide buyers with legitimate intellectual property rights. Richardson notes one of the reasons to do this is to bolster resumes in service of academic advancement.

Richardson has previously identified exploitation of IP systems in the UK, finding thousands of design registrations. His new work identifies 12 instances where design registrations were advertised by a paper mill operating in India and catering to Indian academics.

Richardson’s data shows these design registrations are being advertised as “Australian design patents”. The paper mills sell positions as “owners” of design registrations, charging between $95 and $150 per owner, for up to eight people to be registered on any given design. A design registration application through IP Australia costs $200 in total.

Guardian Australia identified cases where the registrations were listed as patents on CVs.

“They’re using the services of the Australian government to defraud others,” Richardson says. He points to several unusual instances of design registrations.

One Australian design registration, for an “AI based membrane bioreactor for treatment of wastewater”, belongs to six people whom Guardian Australia has traced to research institutes in India. Five of the six were contacted; none responded to requests for comment.

A “GS Collison” is listed under the address for service on the registration, as well as for 11 other design registrations. However, there is no trace online of GS Collison as an entity, and the address listed for it – level 11 in one of Sydney’s Darling Park towers – corresponds to the offices of IAG, an insurance firm. In response to questions from Guardian Australia, an IAG spokesperson noted level 11 is occupied by a series of meeting rooms.

Another example, a “Smart humanoid robot for industrial applications”, includes Dr Nilesh Torwane, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Queensland as a design owner. When contacted by Guardian Australia, Torwane says he “did no design work on the product” but was invited to be named on the design by others listed on the registration. He also noted the registration “never formed part of any claim I have made for professional or academic advancement”.

“I have disclosed the matter proactively to the University and am taking steps to correct the record, including seeking removal of my name from the registration,” Torwane says. Guardian Australia is not suggesting that the registration is not for a legitimate product, only that Torwane was not involved in its design.

When contacted by Guardian Australia, a spokesperson for IP Australia suggested it was not aware of the research paper by Richardson and colleagues.

“IP Australia welcomes any information that may indicate that the designs registration system is not being used for its intended purposes, and we will consider the implications raised by the research paper. However, we have no data to suggest that there is widespread misuse of the Australian designs registration system in the manner suggested.”

Though Richardson’s paper goes some way to exploring how paper mills are operating, the mills remain “shadowy organisations”, according to Prof Adrian Barnett, a metascience researcher at the Queensland University of Technology who has previously published with Richardson.

“It could be some techie kid in their bedroom, or some of them might be larger organisations that even have morning teas and employees of the month,” he says. “Who knows? But we can see they’re making a decent amount of money.”

While Richardson is being interviewed, his phone buzzes again: another advertisement in a WhatsApp group. The organisations are operating at such a scale and speed it’s hard to keep up.

“We’ve still barely scratched the surface,” he says.

The moment I knew: I heard her beautiful laugh again, and all my emotions came flooding back

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 20:00:06 GMT

Eddie Botha felt an easy connection with Jennifer. But when she went away for a trip, he thought that was the end of their growing romance

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

I met Jennifer at a Guy Sebastian concert in Kuala Lumpur in 2005. It was strange I was there because I’m kind of anti-pop music, but we were introduced there by a mutual friend. We didn’t talk that much but I immediately liked Jen and invited her to dinner the following week.

That first date wasn’t in a fancy restaurant and we sat in the corner and talked for over an hour. I liked that she wasn’t at all bothered by the simplicity of the dining room. Being a foreigner in Malaysia, I immediately felt with Jen that there wasn’t as much of a culture gap as I’d felt with others. I could talk to her easily and was struck by her warmth and openness. And it was there that I first heard her laugh beaming out across the room, a pure, joyous sound.

A few weeks later I organised a weekend getaway to Kuantan with my friend Ivan, who had introduced us, and invited Jen along. I remember she was sort of jumping into the waves and fell backwards, and I caught her in my arms. I didn’t let go immediately and then I felt her hand on my shoulder, and then I heard that laugh again. It was a moment of unexpected intimacy that didn’t feel forced or contrived – almost as if nature pushed us towards each other.

After that trip she went away with a girlfriend of hers to Bali and I thought maybe that was the end of things for us. Partly because her friend was a bit butch, I really wondered for a moment whether maybe they had gotten together on that trip – which of course I would have accepted.

Then one day I was just getting home from work when, out of the blue, I saw her name appear on my phone. I was a bit surprised but very excited – we hadn’t spoken for two or three weeks. I hadn’t known I was going to hear from her again.

She told me she’d had a wonderful trip away and had been thinking about me a lot. I expressed how happy I was to hear from her; that I had been thinking about her a lot as well and would love to see her again soon. In my nervousness I made some silly jokes. When I heard her beautiful, pure laugh again, and all my emotions came flooding back, I was certain she was the one for me. It was only a short call but it was enough to tell me everything I needed to know.

After that we started spending more time together and would speak to each other on the phone for hours in the evenings. She stayed over at my place a few times.

I knew Jen was always worried about how any guy would deal with meeting her eccentric father. When I met him, he was very flamboyant – brightly coloured clothes with lots of jewellery and bling. But I really liked him because I’m a bit eccentric myself.

After three or four months, I asked Jen to marry me. She said no at first. She was only 21 at the time and I was 30. But a few months later, as we spent even more time together, she finally said yes, with her dad’s approval.

We’ve been together for almost 20 years now, have two kids and live in Melbourne. Not to say we haven’t had any troubles. I’m the risk-taker and she’s very risk-averse. I think she is the voice of reason whereas I shoot from the hip. But I think she generally trusts my instincts. We have a healthy, balanced relationship.

I love that she’s always believed in me as an artist. When we met in Malaysia I was working as a landscape architect. When we moved to Australia that fell to the wayside, so she encouraged me to venture more into the arts. She brings her business sense to my arts career.

I admire her career as a CFO for a software company – I’ve had to let go of my old-fashioned instinct that the man should be the bread-winner. I am quite paternal and love spending more time with the kids. Our relationship is based on love and caring for each other – but I think our friendship is the real core that keeps us going. And she still has that beautiful, free flowing laugh, which brings our whole family so much joy.

Eddie Botha’s work will feature as part of the Scotch Foundation Art Show, 10-13 September at James Forbes Academy, Scotch College Melbourne

Newcastle’s Matthias Jaissle looks on bright side despite lacklustre Leverkusen defeat

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 19:18:10 GMT

In spite of a 2-1 loss to Bayer Leverkusen, the new head coach at St James’ Park showed signs he is on the right path, and is closing in on Benfica’s Amar Dedic

Reasons to be fearful or cause to be cheerful? Newcastle fans among a crowd in excess of 39,000 at St James’ Park on Saturday had much to debate as they headed home from a slightly underwhelming 2-1 friendly defeat by Bayer Leverkusen.

The bad news is that a suddenly youthful team still coming to terms with life without this summer’s departed stars, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães, look more than a little undercooked before Liverpool’s visit on Premier League duty next Sunday.

Late last year these teams drew a Champions League group stage game in Leverkusen but since then the Germans have reconstructed a then transitional squad and Newcastle dismantled theirs.

Eddie Howe’s sudden departure at the end of July has left Matthias Jaissle, late of Jeddah’s Al-Ahli, to pick up the managerial pieces. Despite this defeat on a day when Leverkusen looked to be playing within themselves, the 38-year-old German is already showing a few, albeit tentative, indications that he just might be able to put one of football’s most complicated jigsaws back together.

If Malick Thiaw, Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa in particular appear re-energised by his coaching, Jaissle’s faith in the 17-year-old Mason Miley, the younger brother of the midfielder Lewis, was fully vindicated as the academy product shone at right-back.

“Mason’s a young lad with the attitude we need; he has the right heart and the right quality,” said Jaissle as he sipped an energy drink intended to replace the body’s lost electrolytes. If only he could find such a simple solution to filling the missing links left by Gordon, Tonali and Guimarães.

At least Dan Burn is still around and will be Newcastle’s captain, with Joelinton as his deputy. The Brazilian, though, is injured and will miss the Liverpool game, while Burn was not involved here as Jaissle split his squad in two during a weekend that features another friendly here, against Strasbourg on Sunday.

Leverkusen represented the new manager’s first match in charge at St James’ Park but it was hardly the ideal start. Inside a minute his team were behind.

When Ibrahim Maza manoeuvred the ball on to his left foot in the area, Newcastle’s new goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, was powerless to resist the resultant shot. No matter that it was only a friendly, even Howe’s normally super-confident successor looked a little crestfallen.

“It’s a big challenge,” he said. “It’s a big transition.”

Jaissle cut a restless figure as he prowled the home technical area, sometimes straying far too far outside its confines for the liking of match officials.

The good news for a coach who promises to prove more entertaining than his team – at least in their current incarnation – was that a reasonably strong starting XI improved incrementally during the first half and equalised shortly before half-time. Jaissle duly greeted Thiaw’s scoring header from Elanga’s corner with a prolonged bout of clapping.

By then he could also reflect favourably on a positive contribution from the Miley brothers. While Lewis looked his customarily assured self in central midfield on his first appearance since breaking a leg last spring, Mason’s efforts at right-back frequently frustrated Leverkusen’s Miguel Gutiérrez.

It seemed thoroughly fitting that the latter was showered with praise from his manager when, late in the second half, he hobbled off with cramp. With England’s Tino Livramento sidelined by calf trouble, Miley Jr is in real contention to start against Liverpool.

Yet in eight days’ time another right-back, Benfica’s Amar Dedic, could well have been added to Newcastle’s squad. The 23-year-old, who can also operate at left-back, previously played for Jaissle at RB Salzburg and, on Saturday night, appeared close to finalising a move to Tyneside.

Once that deal is done attention will doubtless turn to filling the midfield chasm left by Tonali and Guimarães. Although the 18-year-old Sean Steur – one of four players aged 20 or under signed by Newcastle since June – showed off some nice touches, the former Ajax prodigy betrayed his inexperience at times.

Players with more mature presence are clearly required but Marseille’s Pierre-Emile Højbjerg has declined a £13m move to north-east England and João Palhinha is still to be persuaded to leave Bayern Munich to plug the leadership vacuum.

On this evidence Leverkusen’s new manager, Carles Martínez, recently imported from Toulouse, might be reluctant to do a job swap with his Newcastle counterpart. Martínez’s side improved after the second-half introduction of the dangerous forward Patrik Schick and few Newcastle fans would argue the visitors did not deserve to win courtesy of Victor Boniface’s late rolled finish, with that opening created when the Nigerian expertly turned Steur.

How Jaissle, who looks to still be fathoming out how to unlock Nick Woltemade’s real yet still latent talent, could do with similar attacking incision.

Asked if Liverpool were arriving in Toon too soon, he initially replied: “We’ll do our best,” before turning upbeat. “We’ll keep using positivity,” he said. “I like these challenges. We are not concerned. I can’t wait.”

Community Shield offers insight into Arsenal’s desire and Maresca’s Manchester City impact

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 19:00:04 GMT

Wembley curtain-raiser can offer clues but it is no reliable pointer to a season – its winners have not landed the title since 2018

The doubt for anyone when a long-strived-for goal has been achieved is hunger. Arsenal waited 22 years for their 14th league title and, compounding the yearning, finished second three times in a row before finally lifting the Premier League trophy in May. The physical exertions of last season were immense – as seen by Declan Rice’s clear exhaustion and Bukayo Saka’s intermittent contributions at the World Cup, where William Saliba picked up a back injury – but so too was the emotional strain.

The first weeks of a new season after a major tournament, especially the World Cup, are often a little erratic anyway, but this feels like a particularly unpredictable start to a campaign. Nine of the 20 Premier League clubs have changed manager this summer. For the first time in 40 years, none of the five big managerial beasts of the Premier League era – Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola – will be in charge of a club. There are unknowns and uncertainty everywhere, even at Arsenal. Mikel Arteta may be the longest-serving manager in the league but there are questions even there; it would be no great surprise if Arsenal were to start slowly.

Manchester City are at the other end of the scale, after two seasons that were disappointing by their extremely elevated recent standards, and with a new manager after a decade under Guardiola. Enzo Maresca may look like his predecessor and his football may look like a version of his predecessor’s – notably from that period when he was his assistant manager – but he arrives at City surrounded by questions. He led Leicester to promotion and won the Europa Conference League and Club World Cup with Chelsea, but fans of those clubs seemed unconvinced by the style of play. And while Chelsea clearly had problems with the balance of their squad, and got dramatically worse after he left, it wasn’t entirely clear he was making the best of the resources he had.

The Community Shield is a first opportunity to make some kind of assessment of whether Arsenal’s hunger is as sharp as it was last season, and of how City’s squad are adapting to their new manager. It is, though, a largely ceremonial occasion, any lessons drawn to be taken with extreme caution. Not since 2018 have the winners of the Community Shield gone on to win the Premier League; in that sense, it’s a sort of anti-bellwether. Where it can give indicators as to the season ahead tends to be less in showcasing the strengths of a potential champion than in exposing the flaws that might bring a side low.

This year is unlikely to bring a repeat of 1974, when the scrap between Kevin Keegan and Billy Bremner exposed both the Liverpool forward’s unease at the retirement of Bill Shankly and, more consequentially, the general loss of morale at Leeds after Brian Clough had succeeded Don Revie. Often the significance of the Community Shield is properly recognised only in retrospect. José Mourinho was clearly in a strange mood when he turned up for the 2015-16 game unshaven and in tracksuit bottoms and a baggy T-shirt before suffering his first ever defeat to Arsène Wenger. Few suspected, though, the chaos that was about to unspool at Chelsea, culminating with Mourinho’s dismissal that December.

Last season, as Crystal Palace beat Liverpool on penalties after a 2-2 draw, there were abundant indications of what was to come, especially about Arne Slot’s side. Mohamed Salah seemed disconnected from the rest of the forward line. The defence was a mess. Twice they conceded equalisers. Whether they were recognised at the time is another matter; the difficulty is separating teething problems or a team being only partway through their preparation for the new season from longer-term issues that could still be undermining a team two or three months into the season.

There are few obvious questions to which Sunday’s meeting could begin to offer answers. Bruno Guimarães came off the bench for Arsenal in Wednesday’s friendly against Como and could be involved, probably alongside Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield. The 19-year-old has been prominent in pre-season after Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Martin Ødegaard were given extended breaks after the World Cup, but he has been linked with a move. In that context, his celebration after scoring against Como, making a heart sign with his hands and tapping the badge, felt significant.

After the sale of Leandro Trossard, the left side of Arsenal’s attack is in need of strengthening. Morgan Rogers went to Chelsea and Vinícius Júnior stayed at Real Madrid, but they did sign the 24-year-old Greece international Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge. Sunday offers an opportunity to see how he fits in, and whether Arsenal still need another option on that flank.

For City, the biggest personnel issue probably surrounds the future of Rodri, whose proposed move to Barcelona is yet to materialise, which in turn leaves City hanging on a potential replacement. Enzo Fernández appears the preferred candidate but whether his comparative lack of physicality can be accommodated deep in midfield, even after the signing of the robust Elliot Anderson, remains to be seen.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Tijjani Reijnders started friendlies against Inter and Atlético but is on his way to Al-Qadsiah while Bernardo Silva has joined Real Madrid, meaning a significant overhaul of midfield. Whether that includes Phil Foden in the long term is unclear. Since being named player of the year in 2024, he has struggled for form, but started the Inter and Atlético games. As others recover from the World Cup, the next few weeks offer an opportunity to reassert himself.

Given he started only 11 games over the past two seasons, the departure of John Stones probably matters less from a footballing point of view than in the loss of a dressing-room leader. Without Stones and Silva – and Guardiola – the character of the squad cannot but be different.

Sunday constitutes an opportunity to see both what the new City may look like, and how Arsenal have adapted, having at last won the title. But it’s only the Community Shield; any conclusions should be treated with appropriate caution.

Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans gather to pay respects as coffin brought home

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 18:44:49 GMT

Fans line streets, singing Total Eclipse of the Heart ahead of Welsh singer’s Swansea funeral

Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans lined the streets of her home town in south Wales to pay respects to the singer as her coffin was brought back to her former home.

The singer, whose real name was Gaynor Sullivan, died unexpectedly on 8 July in Portugal at the age of 75.

Many fans stood along Newton Road in Mumbles, Swansea, to watch the procession as her coffin was brought back. The coffin was draped in the Welsh flag and accompanied by a framed photograph of the singer.

Fans threw flowers on to the hearse, and the crowd erupted into applause and broke out into a rendition of Total Eclipse of the Heart.

Mumbles was Tyler’s part-time home, as she split her time between Algarve in Portugal and a large Victorian house in Blackpill, near Mumbles, overlooking Swansea Bay.

Tyler became renowned globally for her pop music hits, including Total Eclipse of the Heart and I Need a Hero.

Among those waiting to pay their respects to Tyler was Carys Edwards, 18, who said the singer was “an inspiration to everybody”.

She told PA Media: “Her music touched a lot of people, especially me. I’m quite surprised how many people came here today, but then not as well, because she was such an icon.

“She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans in Wales.

“Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales, we loved her a lot. When we found out she passed away, it was such a heartbreak to all of us. We cried and everything.”

Michael Bone, 58, and his partner Alan Hawkins, 54, travelled from Derby to watch the procession.

“We thought it’d be nice to pay our respects,” said Bone. “For me personally, it’s because in my teens, her music was quite prolific. For me, it was her most iconic period in the 1980s.”

Others were reported to have travelled from as far as Austria to witness the procession of Tyler’s coffin.

Her other hits included It’s a Heartache and If You Were a Woman (And I Was a Man). She represented the UK in the 2013 Eurovision song contest in Malmö, Sweden, with the song Believe in Me, finishing in 19th place.

A celebration of Tyler’s life is set to take place at Swansea Minster (Church of St Mary’s) on Monday 17 August. Only those with invitations will be allowed inside, but the service will be shown on a large screen in nearby St David’s Square – and members of the public can pay their respects.

After the service, Tyler’s coffin will make a final journey through her home village of Skewen – followed by a private gathering strictly for family and friends.

Tyler grew up in a council house in Skewen with five older siblings. “I class myself as a working-class girl, and I’ve never stopped working,” she told the Guardian in 2013. “I do an awful lot [of performances] because I feel other people would love to be offered what I’m offered.”

In her memoir, she wrote fondly of Wales: “I may have done some extraordinary things … but in so many ways, I’m still that young girl from Wales, dancing around the piano with her family, and I always will be.”

At the time of her death, then prime minister, Keir Starmer, said Tyler was an “iconic figure” and “one of Britain’s greatest recording artists”. Others who paid tribute to her included Catherine Zeta-Jones and Cliff Richard.

Moroccan police arrest more than 100 people as they attempt to enter Ceuta

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 18:08:21 GMT

Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory

Moroccan police have arrested 111 people as they tried to enter Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, amid ⁠tightened security on both sides after social media posts ​called for another mass crossing.

The attempted crossing on Saturday came two weeks after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, causing tensions within the EU and prompting anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died trying to ⁠reach European soil.

A source in Morocco’s interior ministry told news agency Reuters that those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city near Ceuta.

Moroccan police used teargas to disperse groups of migrants ⁠gathered on hills about 1.9 miles (3km) from the border, according to Spanish news agency EFE. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plainclothes, returning from the hills outside ​Fnideq.

EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco’s interior ministry ordered their journalists ‌to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.

In Ceuta, ‌Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police patrolled the main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after the deadly crossing attempt on 30 July.

Madrid has ‌since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police officers from mainland Spain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The interior ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.

“We’ll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of 30 July from happening again,” Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Thursday.

About 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, the minister added. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.

Grande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the territory, travel to mainland Spain or ‌obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he added.

Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring “the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin” calling for a mass crossing ​on 15 August, warning it would prosecute organisers and participants.

A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Melilla, another Spanish territory in north Africa.

Body found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George Smyth

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 17:14:38 GMT

Family paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset police

A body has been found in the search for an 18-year-old British man who went missing last year while hiking in Romania, UK police said.

George Smyth, a geology student at the University of Bristol, went missing in November.

On Saturday, Avon and Somerset police said a body found in the region of the country is believed to be that of Smyth.

His family have been informed and are being supported by a family liaison officer, the force added.

Smyth’s family said: “We are all devastated by George’s death.

“He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends.

“We want to thank Salvamont mountain rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George, despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions.

“They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.”

Efforts will be made to return Smyth’s body to the UK once formal identification has taken place.

The family’s statement added: “We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family.

“Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye.

“We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss.”

On Wednesday, mountain rescue teams said they had resumed their search in “previously indicated areas, under rock walls, in grates and in the hard-to-reach sectors” but without success.

The student, from Newport in Shropshire, is believed to have left Poiana Brașov heading to Bran. He reached Țigănești, where he made an emergency call for help.

At the time, rescuers said he was in a “very isolated and hard to access mountain area” and the weather conditions were extremely severe with strong winds, heavy snowfall and dense fog.

The search and rescue operation also involved a canine unit, drones and helicopters being deployed.

Sebastian Marinescu, from the area’s mountain rescue service, previously told the BBC the 18-year-old “was disoriented, physically exhausted, and already showing signs of hypothermia” when they received the emergency call.

Championship roundup: Middlesbrough seal comeback win; West Brom beat Norwich

The Guardian Sat, 15 Aug 2026 16:37:44 GMT

Lankshear ends Lincoln’s nine-month unbeaten run

Millwall start with 2-0 win over 10-man Bristol City

Will Lankshear scored a second-half double on his debut as Middlesbrough fought back to kick off their Championship campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 victory, ending promoted Lincoln’s remarkable nine-month unbeaten run.

The Imps – playing their first second-tier match in 65 years – made a strong start and opened the scoring in the 12th minute through Adam Reach. But the former Tottenham forward Lankshear marked his first league appearance since his move to the Riverside by equalising just after the hour and then stabbing in a stoppage-time winner.

It was a devastating end for Lincoln as a run of 29 games undefeated in all competitions since early December was brought to a halt in their first league match since their new joint head coach partnership of Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw stepped up to take over after the departure of Michael Skubala to Bristol City in May.

Philippe Clement was left feeling extremely hard done by after watching his Norwich side lose 2-1 at home to West Brom. Clement felt his side should have won the game comfortably with the number of chances they created – and also felt Aune Heggebø’s opener, which came against the run of play, should have been ruled out for handball.

“It was clearly with the arm that the player scores – we could see that from where we were watching, 50 yards away,” he said. “It was the decisive moment in the game and should have been spotted. There are four officials and one of them should have seen it. Maybe the referee didn’t have the best view – but the linesman on our side needs to see that. Missing game-changing moments like this shouldn’t happen – it has cost us at least two, maybe three points.”

Norwich were on the front foot for most of the game but could not find a way past a resolute defence, and were made to pay for failing to take their chances as Albion scored two late goals to make it a dream start to the new season.

The visitors went in front on 75 minutes when Callum Styles played in Jimmy-Jay Morgan, whose cross was bundled over the line by Heggebø. With three minutes remaining, Morgan made it two with his third goal since joining the Baggies in the summer, racing clear and working his way into the box before blasting the ball home. Mathias Kvistgaarden nodded home a loose ball as the game entered added time.

Ilias Chair scored twice as QPR came from behind to beat Portsmouth 3-1 and claim their first win at Fratton Park in 26 years. Pompey dominated the opening half an hour and took the lead through Terry Devlin’s long-range screamer. But Rangers scored three times in 15 minutes before half-time.

Jamal Lowe converted a second-half penalty as Sheffield Wednesday made a winning start in League One following relegation with a 2-1 victory at Leyton Orient. The Owls, under new ownership since succumbing to the earliest relegation in English Football League history in February, went ahead through Callum Slattery’s debut goal before Joseph Olowu levelled before the break. But Lowe picked himself up after being fouled in the area by James Morris to fire home from the spot in the 66th minute.

Former Premier League champions Leicester were denied victory at Notts County in their first match since relegation as they were held 1-1. Conor Grant’s late strike cancelled out Jayden Joseph’s second-half opener for Leicester and salvaged a deserved point for the home side.

Ciaron Brown’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued another relegated side, Oxford, earning them a 2-2 draw at newly-promoted MK Dons. Charlie Goode and Aaron Collins gave the Dons a 2-1 half-time lead after Mark Harris had fired the U’s in front before Brown turned home a cross in the fifth minute of added time.

Substitute Gideon Kodua scrambled a stoppage-time winner to seal Luton a 4-3 win at Reading, for whom Jack Marriott scored a first-half hat-trick. Huddersfield’s summer signing Derensili Sanches Fernandes struck twice as they beat AFC Wimbledon 3-0 at home despite the first-half dismissal of Bali Mumba.

Victor Adeboyejo fired a second-half winner as Bromley won 1-0 at Barnsley for their first-ever win in the third tier following promotion.

Cambridge United held off a fightback to beat Wigan 3-2 on the U’s return to League One.

Goals from Kell Watts, Louis Appere and Isaac Heath put the hosts in control but Wigan made a game of it in the last 20 minutes when Sonny Perkins and Akeel Higgins set up a nervy finish.

Blackpool and Wycombe shared the points in an opening day 1-1 draw.

The visitors led for long periods at Bloomfield Road, following an early opener from Fred Onyedinma. This was cancelled out by substitute Finley Munroe, who made an instant impact following his loan move from Middlesbrough last week.

Bradford made a winning start with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Peterborough, who finished with 10 men after David Okagbue’s red card.

Second-half goals from Macaulay Gillesphey and Nick Powell were enough for last season’s play-off semi-finalists to secure three points.

Stockport eased to a sparkling 3-1 win at Plymouth as Jack Diamond scored their opener, helped set up a second for Kyle Wootton and a third for Ryan Glover before Xavier Amaechi gave Argyle a late consolation.

Mansfield made a winning start with a hard-fought 2-1 victory over Doncaster.

Rhys Oates swept home the opener but Rovers levelled four minutes after the break when through Jack Senior before Mansfield deservedly won it in the 74th minute with a free-kick from Louis Reed.

Olly Sanderson bundled home in stoppage time to snatch Stevenage a point in a 1-1 draw at Burton. The former Fulham youngster came off the bench to cancel out Jack Armer’s second-half strike for the Brewers.

Josh Coburn scored twice as Millwall kicked off their campaign with a comfortable 2-0 win over 10-man Bristol City at Ashton Gate. The home side went a man down after 36 minutes when midfielder Adam Randell was shown a second yellow card for a foul to prevent a counterattack.

Five minutes later, Coburn converted a low Ryan Leonard cross from the right with a near-post volley. Coburn then doubled the advantage after 50 minutes, taking advantage of poor defending to score unchallenged with a downward header from 10 yards.

The result meant that Skubala’s reign as City manager has begun with two home defeats, after the shock Carabao Cup exit at the hands of League Two Walsall, and without his side scoring a goal.

Steven Schumacher celebrated Bolton’s first Championship win for seven years after surviving a late scare against Preston. Sam Dalby and Thierry Gale put Bolton in command with first-half goals, but the Preston substitute Jusef Erabi ensured a nervy ending by pulling a goal back in the 86th minute. Liam Lindsay passed up a chance to equalise, heading over in added time, to leave Schumacher a relieved man.

“That’s what this division is all about,” he said. “From being in control of the game we’re happy they missed a sitter at the end not to take away our three points. It’s going to be an exciting ride so strap in.”

Newport and new manager Hayden Mullins enjoyed a dream start to their League Two campaign with a 3-0 home win over newly-promoted Rochdale.

Josh March headed the winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time as 10-man Crewe got the better of nine-man Crawley at the Broadfield Stadium.

Late goals from Isaac Moore, James Connolly and Aaron Pressley did the damage as Walsall secured a fine 3-0 away win over Gillingham.

Grimsby got off to a winning start at the expense of newly-relegated Exeter with a tightly-contested 1-0 triumph at Blundell Park.

Harvey Rodgers gave the hosts the lead 36 minutes in as he got on the end of a corner from Charles Vernam, with the linesman calling it over the line before it was cleared.

Tranmere completed a 2-0 victory over Shrewsbury. Jordan Davies’ first league goal for the club and a Charlie Whitaker wonder strike secured the points in an entertaining opening-day clash at Prenton Park.

Northampton and Swindon played out a goalless draw at Sixfields.
