The Guardian view on Nigel Farage: Clacton cannot acquit him

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:06:32 GMT

Reform won a contrived byelection, but scrutiny continues – while the party increasingly attacks the watchdogs and journalists asking awkward questions

Nigel Farage didn’t attend the count of the byelection he forced upon Clacton. Instead, Reform UK’s leader celebrated his win with supporters at a “Farage Fest”, filmed by a friendly TV channel. For a politician who claims to speak for the people, it was telling that at his triumph he preferred an audience of believers.

Mr Farage won because his toughest opponent on the campaign trail was a comedian in a jumpsuit with a bin on his head. That Count Binface nevertheless won 27% of the vote captured the absurdity of a contest the main parties had boycotted as a Faragist stunt. Reform UK’s leader wanted to turn scrutiny of his finances – notably an investigation into whether he failed to report a £5m gift from an overseas crypto billionaire – into a “fight” with the “establishment”. But the result determined who represents the Essex seat, not whether he broke parliamentary or electoral rules.

There is no drop in enthusiasm among Mr Farage’s Clacton supporters. But he engineered an election in the safest territory – and despite facing no significant competition, had 37% vote against him. If even this part of the country can mobilise a substantial anti-Reform protest vote when the main parties stand aside, then imagine what might be possible in marginals where a mainstream challenger would prove more formidable.

Mr Farage also hasn’t escaped the accountability he was trying to outrun. The parliamentary commissioner for standards suspended the investigation when he stopped being an MP; his re-election means the inquiry has resumed. It covers both the millions from the Thailand-based crypto magnate Christopher Harborne, and alleged undeclared support from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

A mandate is not an acquittal. If the commissioner finds a serious breach of the rules and Mr Farage is suspended for 10 or more Commons sitting days, a recall petition in Clacton would follow. If 10% of electors signed it – roughly 1,500 fewer than voted for Count Binface – another byelection would be triggered. This time Mr Farage would face voters after parliamentary censure and a successful recall campaign, not just, as Labour claimed, reeking of the “stench of sleaze”. With the main parties likely to stand, the anti-Farage vote could also coalesce behind one serious challenger – and present a tougher test.

A disturbing pattern is emerging around Reform’s intimidatory tactics. Questions about its funding are repeatedly answered not openly but by attacking those asking. A parliamentary watchdog becomes a “kangaroo court”; Reform deputy leader Richard Tice’s lawyers seek material that could identify sources behind the Guardian’s investigation; and a prominent Farage ally reportedly hired private investigators to examine a Sunday Times journalist investigating the party’s finances.

This is likely to backfire for Reform. Last September the party was polling 32% nationally. After Mr Farage announced in July that he was triggering a byelection, it dropped from 27% to 24% – squeezed by a resurgent Labour, recovering Conservative party and Restore Britain’s more extreme policies. As even supporters such as Tim Montgomerie acknowledge, a political party built on voters’ grievances has now become increasingly preoccupied with its own grievances about the media, investigations and treatment of Mr Farage. The result is that Reform appears inward-looking, defensive and sleazy. That will probably damage the party more than its angry, divisive nationalism, which demonises minorities and shreds Britain’s traditions of tolerance and pluralism.

The Guardian view on booming poetry sales: Homer, meet the Instapoets

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:05:22 GMT

In an unexpected twist, a Hollywood epic has contributed to Britain’s best-ever half-year in poetry sales

In a short story called Career Move, published in the New Yorker in 1992, Martin Amis imagined a world in which screenwriters wrote for little magazines and earned a pittance while poets were global superstars. Amis’s story, a wonderfully ironic inversion of the time-honoured norm, was surprisingly prescient: the film and TV industries have been struggling, with screenwriters facing contracting outlets for their creations, whereas poets are now big business.

The Bookseller reported recently that poetry sales were at a historic high. Part of the increase can be attributed to Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey, which has made Homer hot: editions of The Odyssey and its prequel, The Iliad, have garnered almost £1m in book sales in the UK this year. (As well as valiantly trying to keep the ailing film industry afloat, Nolan has also created a craze for epic poetry.) But Nolan’s film does not solely account for the boom in poetry sales. Even without the Homer run, sales of poetry texts and anthologies were still up by 7.2% from what was historically already a very high base.

The poets leading the charge are not the traditional behemoths – Berryman and the Brownings, Marvell and Milton, Pope and Pound. These remain acquired tastes, read (if at all) in the beleaguered bowers and tottering towers of organised “Eng lit”. The publishing sensations fuelling the poetic sales surge are “Instagram poets” such as Donna Ashworth, Rupi Kaur, Amanda Lovelace and Lucas Jones, whose collection, I Still Believe in Miracles, has netted £400,000 in sales this year.

The appeal of this new generation lies in their directness. They want to be our new best friend. “Maybe you kinda feel how I feel,” says Jones in the introduction to I Still Believe in Miracles. The American poet Lovelace dedicates her 2022 collection, unlock your storybook heart (she eschews capital letters throughout), to “anyone who feels like they’ve yet to find themselves: i promise it’s not too late”. Lovelace advises readers to practise “self-care before, during and after reading”.

Critics dismiss such work as more therapy than poetry, and argue it should be filed under self-help. Since the emergence of Instapoetry online in the middle of the last decade, a fault line has developed among poets as well as critics. Rebecca Watts’ dismissal in a 2018 article in PN Review, a poetry journal, of poets such as Kaur, Kae Tempest and Hollie McNish as “artless and amateur”, laid bare the divisions. The Instapoets have now successfully migrated to print, but the arguments continue. Is this literature for a post-literate age, or a healthy riposte to canonical poets (mostly “male, pale and stale” in the eyes of their detractors)?

A corrective to the canon is no doubt overdue, and poets who appeal to a young readership beset by mental health issues should not be written off. But there are dangers. In June, Faber published Talking in Bed, a slim anthology of Philip Larkin poems in which there is a sense of Larkin being co-opted by the poetry-as-therapy movement. “He finds a way of admitting and delineating our nagging questions and most complicated feelings,” intones the blurb. The acerbic Larkin would not, one suspects, have appreciated this. Poetry should be allowed to be hermetic as well as accessible, and threatening as well as therapeutic.

Arsenal v Manchester City in Community Shield and athletics gold – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:09:45 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

Long gone are the days of an August football big bang, with all the major men’s leagues starting at 3pm on the Saturday after the Charity Shield. But in the wake of Scotland, the Carabao Cup and the National League (not forgetting assorted European qualifiers and the Super Cup), the venerable Football League itself is back – and with it Matchday live. Emillia Hawkins will look at the fallout from Friday night’s Wolves v Blackburn Championship opener (a repeat of the 1960 FA Cup final for even older nostalgia fans) and all the buildup to the rest of the programme. A Bolton v Preston derby kicks off the day’s second-tier programme, alongside League One and League Two games, though the bulk of matches kick off at the sacred hour of three o’clock. Oh, and she will also have all the latest transfer news and gossip across the men’s and women’s games. Send your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com

Football, and lots of it. The pick of the Championship matches is perhaps Middlesbrough v Lincoln: a side who just missed a return to the promised land hosting one that got there. Imps fans have not seen fulfilment of the spring’s “Tottenham away, olé, olé” chant but, having not played at this level since 1961, they will hardly be complaining at facing a club who were in the Premier League in 2016-17, the season that City won promotion from the National League. Scott Murray will have news from the Riverside and all the other grounds, starting with the end of the lunchtime kick-offs, with Leicester’s second ever season in the third tier starting at playoff-winning Notts County among the early League One games.

It’s the penultimate night at the Alexander Stadium in Birmingham and there will be high home hopes for the men’s 100m relay at 9.33pm, after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu completed a British one-two in the individual event. A quarter of an hour later, Amy Hunt, the women’s double sprint gold medallist, will be targeting relay glory. Other British hopefuls include Amber Anning in the women’s 400m at 8.10pm and Jake Wightman in the men’s 1500m at 9.07pm. While Sean Ingle reports from the second city, Luke McLaughlin will guide you through the evening as it happens.

Emillia Hawkins will be back after her Saturday morning stint to pick through that day’s events and look forward to an afternoon of action that includes the traditional Wembley curtain raiser. To the surprise of some, the Community Shield is taking place in Cardiff – not because the FA forgot to book Wembley but, it seems, because four nights of concerts from the Weeknd were more lucrative. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your views on whether Arsenal v Manchester City in what is now a glorified friendly carries any real significance for the new season, and anything your spies can tell us about Watford v Southampton and Burnley v West Ham.

The champions take on the FA Cup winners as usual, but at the Principality Stadium for the first time since 2006, when Liverpool beat Chelsea 2-1. Twelve months ago the Reds were also taking part but went down on penalties to Crystal Palace after a 2-2 Wembley draw in which they led twice and a shootout in which Mohamed Salah disappointed with the opening kick, a set of circumstances that did, in fact, prove a harbinger of what was to come (albeit for a side who were very much still coming to terms with the death of Diogo Jota). This year Arsenal and post-Pep Manchester City lock horns, with Rob Smyth on minute-by-minute duty, while Ben Fisher and Ed Aarons report from the Welsh capital.

The Championship game of the weekend is deemed by Sky to be a claret-and-blue derby, and a first English league game for Burnley’s new manager, the Belgian Nicky Hayen, a much-travelled coach in his 12th role in 13 years. In the away dugout is Nuno Espírito Santo, who couldn’t quite keep West Ham up last season. After five years of Burnley yo-yoing between the top two divisions, Hayen will have his work cut out to engender much optimism in a support base that knows too much about false dawns, while the visitors are in turmoil over events in the boardroom as well as on the pitch. Tim de Lisle is on the blog, and Will Unwin reports from Lancashire.

It’s the last night of action in Birmingham and it could be a triumphant one for Britain, with a rack of relays. Donald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losers

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:03:05 GMT

The pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted them

It’s a shame Nigel Farage ducked the announcement of his victory in the Clacton byelection, which confirmed his return as MP for the seat he had needlessly resigned from just a few weeks earlier. You’d have thought he would have loved it. It was the culmination of a stunt, an exercise in politics as performance. It was a display animated by – and seeking to inflame – grievance, a million miles away from the hard, grinding work of tackling the problems that underlie those grievances. It was an attempt to deflect scrutiny, distract attention and evade responsibility. It was, in other words, everything nationalist populists like him excel at. Indeed, the only thing.

Reform UK said Farage stayed away because Essex police had warned of a “credible threat” to his security, a claim swiftly denied by Essex police. (Add a flexible approach to the truth to that list of nationalist populists’ talents.) Still, it was a slightly odd claim to make. Recall Farage’s favoured explanation – there are others – for the undeclared £5m gift he received from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, which prompted the very parliamentary investigation that so riled the Reform leader he felt compelled to quit his seat and seek a preemptive not guilty verdict from the people of Clacton: namely, that he needed the money to pay for private, enhanced security. It seems £5m was not quite enough to ensure the lucky recipient would be safe standing next to a man dressed as a bin.

Unless, maybe, security was not the whole story. Farage also said he skipped the count because he didn’t want to be “demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”. Quite right. If Nigel Farage is to be demeaned and humiliated, it should be by people of standing. As it happens, he may get his wish. Now that he’s an MP again, the probe into the multiple financial questions that surround him, including over the undeclared support he received from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell, has resumed. A finding against him could necessitate yet another byelection, except this time the major parties will not repeat their boycott and he will have to do battle with opponents even more formidable than an aristocratic trash can.

Naturally, Farage regards the likes of Count Binface and Baron von Thunderclap as beneath him, perhaps because it would be painful to admit the crucial thing they all have in common. To understand what that is, look no further than the man who is both Farage’s hero and the exemplar of nationalist populism.

Ten years ago, less than five months after the Brexit referendum that represents Farage’s greatest triumph, Donald Trump rode a similar wave of US discontent with the status quo and did it in a similar way – by railing against an ill-defined establishment that had ruined everything. A vote for him would make it all better because, as Trump put it: “I alone can fix it.” In 2024, he was elected once again, on a similar promise.

That victory proved Trump’s mastery of a certain strain of politics. His gift for seizing public attention, for channelling a society’s collective anxieties and for persuading people that a simple remedy is at hand, is unrivalled. While Farage plays the same tunes, Trump is the virtuoso.

And yet, look at what happens once the carnival of the campaign is over and the governing begins. Trump’s record is disastrous. He was elected to tackle inflation, which he claimed was out of control under Joe Biden, but inflation is higher now than it was in November 2024, when he defeated his predecessor. Petrol prices, the indicator Trump repeatedly invoked on the stump in 2024, have leapt up. This, more than any other single factor, helps explain why Trump’s approval ratings have cratered, falling to just 34%.

And yet Trump, whose appeal centred on his persona as a successful businessman – a persona that held, despite a career of failure and serial bankruptcy – is doing almost nothing to improve the economic fortunes of those who voted for him. I don’t mean that he’s trying to pull various policy levers and they’re not working. I mean he’s not trying. As Jonathan Swan, co-author of Regime Change, an eye-popping account of the first 15 months of this second Trump term, told me for the Politics Weekly America podcast: “He’s bored by economic policy.”

Of course, those petrol prices did not rise all by themselves. What drove up the price of oil was the decision that seems set to define this presidency: the war on Iran that began on 28 February. It has proved a calamity. It has failed to achieve any of the admittedly shifting goals Trump declared for it: there has been no regime change in Tehran; Iran’s nuclear threat remains unchecked, while its nuclear ambition is now surely greater, if only to deter a repeat of that US-Israeli attack. And it has barely set back Iran’s conventional capability, judging by the regime’s continuing ability to strike its neighbours. As if all that were not bad enough, Trump has succeeded in making the Iranians stronger than they were on 27 February, by handing them an economic weapon of mass disruption, a chokehold on the global economy in the form of their control of the strait of Hormuz.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Trump can do the performance, claiming to have “obliterated” the enemy one moment or to have made a breakthrough peace deal the next – but performance is all it is. While the Iranian missiles keep coming, the US military is fast running out of the munitions it needs either to intercept or hit back. Trump’s top general warned him of this danger from the start, but Trump waved away those objections, convinced that the war would be over quickly. Trump’s gut told him that Iran would go the way of Venezuela, that it would be fast and easy. His gut was wrong.

It keeps happening the same way. Trump will announce an agreement with Iran or between Hamas and Israel, only for it rapidly to become clear that no deal has been done. Trump lacks the patience for the long, painstaking, detailed work such diplomacy requires. He wants the sugar-rush of a social-media post or a headline. Put simply, he is a maestro of politics as it is now conducted, but he is useless at governing.

In this, the nationalist populists who take their lead from Trump are no different. They are good at raging at how things are, but incapable of making them better. They can articulate resentment and exploit grievance, but they cannot cure the ills that fuel that unhappiness. This, ultimately, is what unites Farage with Trump and indeed with those 33 “nobodies” who fought the byelection in Clacton. They are all protest candidates. It’s just that some of them get elected.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Smart glasses controversy sidelines the benefits for disabled people

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:22:59 GMT

Guardian readers reflect on the ableism rife in the debate about Ray-Ban Meta eyewear, despite the life-changing difference they can make

Your editorial on Meta’s smart glasses acknowledges their value to blind and visually impaired people, then asks that this “not be allowed to distract” from the harms (The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot, 10 August). As an optometrist who owns a small independent practice, I’d suggest that it is visually impaired people who are being treated as the distraction.

I was reluctant to stock Ray‑Ban Meta, having no fondness for Meta or Luxottica, but colleagues persuaded me of the benefits for people with sight impairment. The reality has surpassed that. The majority of our buyers have a visual impairment or learning difficulty. One man, practically illiterate, now has the world read to him.

For many of these patients, leaving the house is already an act of courage. Unfamiliar streets, unreadable signs, the constant low-level anxiety of navigating a world built for the fully sighted. These glasses have quietly made that easier. A week of coverage branding them “pervert glasses” has now added a new anxiety: not whether they can manage the journey, but whether strangers will assume the worst of them for wearing the thing that makes it possible.

A colleague of mine was recently branded a misogynist online, by another optometrist, simply for suggesting the glasses were useful. Opening a Guardian leader with a nickname worthy of a Murdoch red-top – “pervert glasses” – makes that hostility respectable.

The harms you describe are real and worth regulating. But on a recent holiday I left my own pair in the hotel room, yet watched hundreds of people photographing poolside on their phones, my daughters frequently in the background, with no permission sought and no bans imposed. The glasses at least announce themselves with a recording light. Pubs, parks and beaches are indeed not film sets, but they have been full of cameras for 20 years. Regulate by all means. Just remember who ends up wearing the stigma. Aled BrassingtonRomiley, Greater Manchester

Much of the coverage of Meta’s smart glasses has been dominated by the language of “spy glasses” and “predator glasses”, while disabled people’s experiences have barely featured. To its credit, your recent report recognised how useful the glasses can be for blind and disabled people (‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinion, 6 August). Even so, accessibility still feels like a side issue in the wider debate around smart glasses.

I have severe muscular dystrophy and cannot pick up or operate a smartphone. My Ray-Ban Meta glasses let me make calls, send WhatsApp messages, take photos and record moments by voice. I can start a video call without touching a phone. These are not gimmicks. They give me independence and help keep me connected and safe.

I can’t speak for Mark Zuckerberg or defend Meta’s wider record on privacy. But I’ve met Meta developers and scientists working on accessibility. Their commitment is real. They are listening to disabled people and building features that can change lives.

There are legitimate privacy concerns. Secretly filming anyone is unacceptable. Meta should improve the recording light, prevent people disabling it, act against abusive content and be clearer about data use. Regulation must keep up.

But it is wrong to treat everyone wearing these glasses as suspicious, or to impose blanket bans that may exclude disabled people who rely on them for communication, information or safety. Venues can ban recording without banning the glasses themselves.

Phones, doorbells, dashcams and other cameras can all be misused. The answer is to tackle misuse, not demonise a technology or the people who depend on it. Many disabled people are tired of seeing this demonisation while our voices remain absent from the debate raging around smart glasses. We should not have to choose between privacy and independence. We should insist on both. Colin HughesLondon

As it happens, I am visually impaired and find smart glasses very useful. They enable me to read menus and notices and will even translate foreign notices for me. However, I consider recent moves to ban these products from certain premises to be ludicrous.

There have been cases of people using smartphones for illicit purposes, for example surreptitiously filming up women’s skirts. However, nobody has dubbed smartphones “pervert phones” or sought to ban them. Some of the same premises which are now trying to do this to smart glasses also have CCTV, which films everybody without their consent, as do many cameras in our streets including doorbell cameras and dash cams.

I am sure that the vast majority of smart glasses wearers use the product responsibly and would not dream of filming people without their consent. The theoretical possibility that they might do something bad is not a reason to ban the product entirely. You might as well ban the sale of kitchen knives, in case we use them to stab each other, or even cars in case we use them to run somebody over!Dr Alastair ForbesBridport, Dorset

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:22:19 GMT

Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss find the humour in having the same name and working for the same company

At least the Guardian’s Ewan Murray and Sky Sports’ Ewen Murray work for different outlets (A tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identity, 8 August). Stephen Moss (former literary editor, and chess and classical music expert) and I (Birdwatch columnist) both write for the Guardian, causing endless confusion.

A member of Sedgemoor chess club once told me that “We would be very honoured if you could come and give us a game” (they wouldn’t), while a woman, after admitting that she “quite enjoyed” my birding articles, spoiled it by adding “but when you write about classical music, it’s absolutely wonderful!”

With reference to Ewan Murray’s article about meeting Ewen Murray, and the two being mistaken for each other, these days I have resigned myself to being “the other Stephen Moss”.

I manage to write a book about once a decade (at best), usually on some minority pursuit such as chess or cricket. The real, remarkably productive Stephen Moss knocks off bestsellers every other month. The Owl, The Robin, The Swan, The Swallow, The Wren. There are 11,000 bird species. That’s a lot of potential books. But I am NOT bitter.

We are about the same age and, though we have never met, have tracked each other’s careers closely. He wrote for BBC Wildlife; I wrote for BBC Music magazine. The BBC sometimes used to send me his cheques as payment for pieces. Always very welcome. We have both had long associations with the Guardian.

I get very tempting offers of birdwatching holidays across Europe and the US. One day I will accept one, even though I can barely tell a buzzard from a blackbird. I frequently get emails, with a detailed description, reporting a rare bird that a Guardian reader has seen on their local lake. My stock response is to say it’s a short-eared Siberian warbler – the first one seen in the UK since 1711 – and they should report it to the RSPB.

It could all have been so different. Radio 5 Live once confused us and asked me to appear to discuss the killing of garden birds by domestic cats. I politely pointed out their mistake, but now realise what I should have done: go on and welcome this bird massacre. That would have caused a dent in the real, annoyingly successful Stephen Moss’s reputation and sales, leaving me to rule the roost. But I am not bitter!Stephen MossSurbiton, London

Life in the theatre is most revealing

Cathy Scott-Willars responds to an article about the secret lives of theatre workers

I enjoyed your article (The secret lives of theatre workers: ‘People were having full sex in the stalls’, 9 August). I worked many roles front of house and later as operations manager at a busy regional theatre, and it has provided me with some of the most entertaining stories.

My favourite was working at a performance of The Rocky Horror Show in the large main theatre, while in the smaller studio was a play aimed at teenagers. The programming team had provided some post-show entertainment in the form of a DJ and breakdancer for the studio show, which happened to time with the interval of Rocky Horror. The scene I was met with was an usher crying, a furious college tutor shouting at her because her students had witnessed a man in a corset and thong attempt breakdancing, and his balls had fallen out, exposing himself.

Another moment that stayed with me was locking the building up at the end of the night. I was late doing my lockdown and was on autopilot, knocking on dressing room doors and popping my head round to ensure everyone had gone. As I swung open one door, not giving the recipient time to answer, I walked in on Rufus Hound in his pants! Mortified, I apologised and quickly closed the door, while worrying I may get into trouble. Instead he passed on a message at stage door to apologise for leaving late and giving me a fright. What a nice guy.

Sadly, audience aggression towards front-of-house staff was commonplace, and after three years as an operations manager, I decided it was time to move on. Cathy Scott-WillarsPrestatyn, Denbighshire

There may be something in the argument identified by Andy Beckett that increased use of ebikes reflects broader changes in urban areas, including the cost of housing (Lime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation?, 8 August). Yet none of that excuses the sheer impunity that radiates from ebike users, worsened by the design of city bikes which encourage the rider to sit back as if on a magic steed from which to survey their kingdom.

Their irresponsibility imposes externalities on other road users and pedestrians: riding through red lights and across junctions with no heed to other traffic, wearing headphones (but seemingly never helmets), being on the phone or apparently scrolling while riding, carelessly weaving just to maintain a conversation, riding far too fast on paths shared with pedestrians, dropping bikes like litter. As for riding home after drinking in the pub – seriously?

As a helmet-wearing cyclist, it is maddening to dodge people who seem barely familiar with a bike, let alone being in traffic. The behaviour needs to change. In the first instance, that must be through regulation and for riders and suppliers to be liable for the consequences of their actions, which sadly are sometimes serious. Kevin LloydHighbury, London

Digested week: Humid New York or London’s oven-blast heat? Tough one to call

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:01:56 GMT

Plus, heartbreakingly brilliant Cats: the Jellicle Ball, summer reads and Taylor Swift’s low-key wedding

I’ve been in New York for two weeks, where the unthinkable has happened. Even for a city accustomed to extremes, it is so hot, so humid, so reminiscent of Mobile in Alabama, or Mumbai that, all over New York, people have been forced to break persona to talk about the weather. “Was it always like this?” (No.) “Can you believe this?” (No.) “Are you having a stroke?” (Possibly.)

Received wisdom has it that heatwaves in Britain and Europe are worse than in the US because we don’t have air conditioning, but as I write this, on my first day back in heatwave London, it’s a tough one to call.

If the south of England feels like Riyadh, with its oven-blast of dry heat, New York comes with total humidity. It is so dense, so impenetrable, so vastly more furnace-like than any previous summer that it makes you angry just walking down the street.

Air conditioning takes the edge off, but it’s like trying to disguise medicine with a mouthful of Coke; it only goes so far. Meanwhile, the sweat pours down your back and the sky burns white.

New Yorkers are about as keen to complain about the weather as they are to point out a celebrity, but in these conditions you can’t not talk about it. While the mayor’s office discusses plans to extend cooling systems to subway platforms, individuals devise strategies to be outside for as little time as possible – like Minnesotans planning a trip across town in a snowstorm.

At least the hospitals are temperature-controlled. In Britain, where nurses keel over with heat exhaustion, it can feel, at times, as if the single adequately air-conditioned space is the Apple Store; only the iPhones stay cool.

Current trends in New York that may or may not make it over here: frozen yoghurt is having a resurgence but it’s the posh kind – Greek, not Pinkberry. The newest snack craze is “dot cake”, an $11 cube of dry sponge topped with icing and hundreds and thousands and served in a cup, which, according to the New York Times, New Yorkers have been lining up at 6am all summer to buy. Not at our local Gourmet Garage, I will say).

Beyond food, two things worth mentioning: “dog Crocs”, seen on several pets in the street to protect their paws from the punishing heat of the pavement and, as the name implies, tiny canine versions of their owner’s shoes, only these come in a four-pack.

And on Broadway, Cats: The Jellicle Ball, a heartbreakingly brilliant interpretation of the original show in which a tired-seeming vehicle, badly damaged by the terrible film version, gets a radical makeover. Jellicle Ball is set in the Black and Latino drag pageants of the 1980s ballroom scene and is led by two legendary performers, André De Shields, who at 80 still brings it, and Junior LaBeija, who many will recognise from the classic 1991 documentary Paris Is Burning. The costumes, by Qween Jean, and choreography by Omari Wiles and Arturo Lyons, all rightfully won Tony’s.

As Andrew Lloyd Webber says, it’s criminal the show closed early last week. It’s the best thing I’ve seen for years. Anyway we went, we screamed, we clacked the massive Jellicle Ball fans and at intermission, the theatre played DJ Murphy’s ballroom remixes of Lloyd Webber’s songs while people lost their minds. Pray it comes to London.

How did you eclipse? We were circling Heathrow in the air with the sun behind us when the sky became marginally less sunny. I will add it to the drawer of memories of other, underwhelming eclipse experiences, including that big one in 1999, when I was stuck on a motorway in France and everyone pulled over, looked up at the sky, then got back into their cars. And the Great American Eclipse of two years ago, when I stood in a big crowd and everyone turned to one another and said: “Is that it?” It’s worse than bird watching.

After it’s all over, there is a lot of anticlimactic posting on social media, although a friend in Spain sends a video and they seem to have enjoyed the real thing. As with so many things, I think the enjoyment is chiefly in the anticipation and the pretext it gives everyone to hang out, however briefly, in a single, unifying experience – and the opportunity to do crafts.

My summer reading is haphazard but heartfelt, and I’m flipping between Playworld, Adam Ross’s excellent, coming-of-age novel set in Great Neck, New York; Once the Deed Is Done by Rachel Seiffert, a brilliant examination of camps for displaced people in Germany after the second world war; and Caroline Fraser’s biography of Laura Ingalls Wilder. The book I’ve loved most so far this summer, however, is a reread of Elizabeth Jane Howard’s memoir, Slipstream, and now I’ve gone down the wormhole and want to read everything she ever wrote.

The writer died in 2014, at the age of 90, and is best known for the Cazalet Chronicles, but Slipstream is a piece of social and literary history it’s hard to match. Given how a great central theme of the book is Howard’s low self-esteem, what’s interesting is how bold she was, insisting on a life that met none of the requirements of her time and class; despite a very well-to-do background which ensures the book is stuffed with cameos by people called Minky and dinner-party guests who, she might add casually, “was home secretary at the time”, Howard bolted out of three marriages, left her child in the care of others, and lived for many years a rackety, bohemian existence characterised by lack of funds and adventurous, penniless travel. Quite apart from her writing talent, it’s a study in courage and resolve.

It’s been six weeks since the wedding of Taylor Swift to Travis Kelce and, amazingly, no one has cracked. All the NDAs are holding! The only public utterance about the event has been from Kelce himself, who said the wedding had been “the best night of my life”, which was “full of a lot of celebration”. Perhaps this is what happens when so many of the guests are near-strangers who simply feel grateful for the invitation.

None of the rest of us, meanwhile, will ever forget it; the spectacle of people who’d met the bride and groom once, if at all, dropping everything to scurry across the country or the Atlantic to celebrate the big, celebrity wedding next to Penn Station. It’s hard, in hindsight, to put your finger on who the most embarrassing attendee was, but I’d say Hugh Grant was right up there, as well as Tom Hanks, and Andrew Scott, most of whom seem to have met Swift backstage at the Eras tour in 2024 – or possibly the Toy Story 5 premiere in 2026 – since when, I guess, they’d forged meaningful friendships. Oh, to be world famous, and have this as your life.

So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows it

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 10:29:27 GMT

The Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bear

Nigel Farage is a rattled, embattled politician. Perhaps he feels buoyed up by securing slightly more votes in a byelection boycotted by all the main parties than he did in the general election two years ago. That was despite 10,000 fewer people turning out to vote. But there was never any question that he was going to win a byelection he called purely to deflect scrutiny of his undeclared £5m personal gift from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and donations from a convicted fraudster.

Farage chose Clacton as his parliamentary launchpad for a reason. It was here that his previous outfit, Ukip, secured its breakthrough in the byelection of 2014. It is one of the most pro-leave seats in Britain, while Electoral Calculus estimates that almost no other constituency is this rightwing.

When I visited, I found no shortage of voters who were defiant about Farage’s scandals. They saw no problem with a politician being showered with dosh by a foreign-based billionaire, arguing that Farage deserved it because he was a “nice man” and even suggesting he might invest it locally. They bought the narrative that the establishment was out to get their man, as if a millionaire ex-City broker who is a sometime friend of the US president is some plucky outsider.

They are representative of about a fifth of the country who laud Farage as the mainstream politician most hostile to immigration, and who are contemptuous of a Conservative party that failed even on its own terms in office. What should concern Farage, however, is that most Britons are more opposed to him than ever, and are determined to block him from power. That majority delivered victory to the Greens in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, and to Andy Burnham in June’s Makerfield byelection.

That the parody candidate Count Binface won more than a quarter of the vote in this ultra-rightwing heartland is a warning in itself. Yes, this “independent space warrior” secured plenty of media attention, but he had precious little ground game – that is, an army of volunteers to get out the vote. Many voters I spoke to hadn’t even heard of him. It seems plausible that some of those who made Count Binface the most successful joke candidate in history had previously voted not just Labour, Lib Dem or Green, but Conservative too.

Farage refused to attend the official declaration of this election he chose to call. That suggests not just petulance and contempt for his own voters, but the insecurities of a jittery man. He claims Essex police had told him about an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”, but the local force said there had been no “incidents or issues” related to the byelection and that attendance was up to candidates. And did Farage not claim that his £5m personal gift was needed to pay for his security?

The explanation is probably more mundane. Being mocked on stage by a man in a bin does not exactly provide the optics of a heroic struggle against the establishment.

What next for the Farage show? If he thought the byelection was an effective ruse to deflect from his money issues, reality caught up with him quickly. The parliamentary watchdog has now reopened its investigation into Farage’s gift and donations, and another byelection may be forced if there is an adverse ruling.

But it is not just finances that have plunged Reform UK into crisis. Farage’s proud association with Donald Trump – toxic even to most Reform voters – has become an ever greater drag. Absorbing so many former Conservatives was surely another big error. The last government was bitterly rejected for a reason, not least by Farage’s own supporters, and filling Reform’s ranks with its former leading lights hardly helped the party’s anti-establishment pretences.

And then there is the pivot to ever more toxic rightwing politics, perhaps partly driven by pressure from the even further right Restore Britain, founded by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Farage now talks of “anti-white discrimination” – rhetoric once confined to the ugliest reaches of the far right. His talk of “pure cold rage” after the conviction of Henry Nowak’s murder – just hours before riots over it – rightly disturbed many.

Then there’s Zia Yusuf, his home affairs spokesperson, whose increasingly aggressive social media posts speak to Reform’s authoritarian underbelly. Yusuf repeatedly describes his opponents as “traitors” – his latest target was the Tory former defence secretary Ben Wallace – and threatens that an unspecific “reckoning is coming”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

All of this alarms most Britons, who have concluded that Reform must be kept from power and will vote tactically if needs be. Yet this is of scant comfort to the absurdly underscrutinised Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, because Reform’s hardened core shows no interest in returning to her camp. Rightwing Britain, then, is divided.

It would be a mistake to write Farage off, however. We are in the midst of the Andy Burnham bounce. Voters are relieved to be rid of Keir Starmer, and for now Labour is tempting back some progressive voters who defected to the Greens. But Burnham has yet to be forced into many big decisions. Britain’s economic plight, its crisis-stricken public services and Burnham’s slowness to hike taxes on the booming rich could all come to a head in October’s budget. Disillusionment could swell, and Reform could benefit – unless, of course, Burnham calls a snap election first.

But you have to ask whether Farage’s heart is really in this. Reports that he received his £5m gift after saying he would need “a million a year” to serve as an MP are telling. Here is a man who appears to enjoy the high life and feel parliamentary politics damages his earning potential. He seems increasingly riled by the sort of scrutiny he has long managed to avoid. Perhaps, after a pointless triumph over a bin, he may simply decide he has had enough.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

How can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars?

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 07:00:21 GMT

Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of us

In this fragmented but supposedly mild country, watching and talking about the weather forecast is meant to be a reassuring, unifying activity. Collectively, we have created and maintained a national climate narrative of small disappointments and pleasures. The first weather forecaster to appear on British TV, George Cowling, made his debut on the BBC in January 1954, predicting that “tomorrow would be rather windy”, but “a good day to hang out the washing”. For most of the 72 years since, such brief, carefully calibrated broadcasts have provided people from Aberdeen to Penzance with practical information, small talk and minor grumbles about essentially the same situation: living in a country where the weather is constantly changing, in a paradoxically unchanging way.

Yet like the traditional British climate, that common weather culture may now be evaporating. “Met Office considers issuing red ‘extreme heat warning’ across Britain while nation enjoys ‘incredible summer’,” said the headline above the forecast on the GB News website on Monday, caught between terror and delight at the latest heatwave. As the climate crisis has affected this country in more and more unmistakable but uneven ways, TV weather forecasters have increasingly struggled to find the right language to describe this transformation’s daily consequences. Their struggle influences and exemplifies that of many Britons to understand, and work out what we think about, the apparent end of the weather patterns we expected to shape our whole lives.

Across all the British TV broadcasters, sometimes within the same bulletin, or even the same sentence, weather forecasters now present sunshine as welcome and oppressive; high temperatures as miraculous and unbearable; rain as an inconvenience and desperately needed; cloud cover as depressing and a relief. Tanned forecasters in sundresses, emphasising the positives for domestic holidaymakers of another record-breaking summer, alternate with grim-faced forecasters suggesting we are experiencing a weather apocalypse.

Meanwhile, the wildly differing effects of the climate crisis on different areas, and from one season to another, are further fracturing Britain’s weather conversation into a babble of separate, sometimes conflicting discourses. This year, parts of the country have experienced such contrasting summers – wetter than usual in western Scotland, desert-like in southern England – that we can no longer say they share broadly the same northern European climate, as had been assumed for centuries. In an era of separatism and nationalism, another major binding element of the UK may be falling away.

Beneath the relatively placid surface of our previous weather culture, there were always some tensions and contradictions. In a 2025 academic paper, British Heatwave Discourse (1985–2023): from Ice Cream to Armageddon?, Thijs van Dooremalen and Philip Smith analysed articles about heatwaves in the national press. They found that until 2000 positive and negative coverage coexisted in roughly equal quantities, “often in the same newspaper”. From 2000 to 2014, the balance shifted slowly towards the negative, as the climate crisis became a mainstream worry. Yet only from 2015 did an “Apocalyptic genre” of heatwave articles begin to become dominant; and a “Romantic genre” of celebratory coverage remains. In a country where many people still spend much of the year feeling cold, the idea of hot weather as a liberation is likely to linger, for some, for decades to come.

For other Britons, heatwaves have become political flashpoints, their causes to be furiously contested, their existence even denied. During the record heat of 2022, “weather forecasters faced unprecedented levels of trolling”, the BBC reported, including “hundreds of abusive tweets or emails questioning their reports and telling them to ‘get a grip’… ‘it’s just summer’”. Some of these climate crisis deniers described advice on how to stay cool as “pandering to the ‘woke brigade’”, and accused the BBC and Met Office of “scaremongering” to help the then Conservative government impose unneeded green policies.

This summer, some of these conspiratorial arguments have re-emerged. But with the Tories having in effect turned against net zero, joined by Reform UK, Restore Britain and most of the rightwing media, disagreeing with weather forecasters who express alarm about our changing climate has become more mainstream. Discussing the weather is no longer just small talk, but also a battlefield in the culture wars.

No wonder forecasters often sound unsure or extremely cautious about what tone to adopt on air. In 2023, the BBC’s Tomasz Schafernaker gave a very careful interview to the Big Issue. “While our language remains largely the same,” he said, “we have adapted it to include references to climate change. We must be mindful that prolonged periods of sun and heat are not always good news … However, there are often areas in the UK where the weather is much more comfortable, [so] highlighting that it’s not ‘all bad’ is important. It’s a balance that we assess on a daily basis.”

Yet three years on, his broadcasts have become less neutral. “The savage summer continues across Europe,” he said on the BBC weather website last Thursday afternoon. “It’s been excruciatingly hot …” On BBC One last Sunday evening, while giving this week’s UK forecast, he kept making gestures of helplessness and disbelief. It was like a weather bulletin from a dystopian drama.

Such interventions no longer seem melodramatic. “The climate of the 20th century has now gone,” says Mike Kendon, a Met Office scientist and co-author of State of the UK Climate in 2025, published last month. So far, this year’s weather has been more extreme. Even more than the heat, summer drought and winter floods, its key feature has been the weather getting stuck in one state for months – a characteristic of harsh continental climates, rather than the changeable one around which our society has been built. So it’s possible that next summer will feature relentless rain, not drought, and that other seasons will continue to stall as well, damaging the economy, everyday life and public health.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Britons are world famous for their weather stoicism. But this stoicism has been created by centuries of relatively minor weather discomforts and disasters. How the forecasters, and the rest of us, will react as the climate crisis intensifies – in our private behaviours and assumptions as well as our public lives – is a question we are only in the early stages of answering.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Prosecutors Examined Firm With Tie to Judge in Trump Hush-Money Trial

The New York Times August 15, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The U. S. attorney in Chicago subpoenaed a fund-raising firm that had been co-owned by the daughter of Judge Juan Merchan, who conducted the trial that led to Donald Trump’s felony conviction.

By Glenn Thrush

Reporting from Washington

The U. S. attorney’s office in Chicago has spent the past year investigating a Democratic fund-raising firm once co-owned by the daughter of the judge in President Trump’s hush-money trial in New York, according to court filings and people familiar with the inquiry.

Last August, the U. S. attorney, Andrew S. Boutros of the Northern District of Illinois, directed Authentic Campaigns Inc. to turn over a broad range of internal communications with clients. They included former Vice President Kamala Harris, former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, and the Democratic National Committee, according to a grand jury subpoena reviewed by The New York Times.

Loren Merchan, the daughter of Juan Merchan, a supreme court judge in Manhattan, was the firm’s vice president until late 2024 and was also on the list. The Merchan family has been a frequent target of Mr. Trump and his allies, who have made unsubstantiated claims that the judge was out to get him and that his daughter profited from accusations aired at the trial.

The trial ended with Mr. Trump’s conviction in 2024, in the midst of his campaign for a second term, on 34 felony counts stemming from his efforts to keep a porn star from publicizing her story of a liaison with him.

The firm’s legal team, which included Preet Bharara, the former top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, sought to limit the request. Prosecutors eventually modified the subpoena, narrowing it to focus on a $468 payment from Ms. Harris’s presidential campaign, and emails between Ms. Merchan and her father, according to people with knowledge of the inquiry who requested anonymity to discuss an ongoing legal matter.

It is not clear where the investigation stands. No follow-up subpoenas have been issued to individuals, including Ms. Merchan, suggesting that prosecutors might not be actively working to charge anyone, those people added.

The inquiry is the latest indication of the extent to which U. S. attorneys’ offices across the country, once largely removed from political machinations in Washington, have increasingly been drawn into Mr. Trump’s effort to target his adversaries.

In this case, prosecutors sought the subpoena that came from a criminal referral from Republicans on the House Judiciary Committee. The panel made the referral after Mike Nellis, the founder of Authentic Campaigns, refused to provide the committee with confidential emails it was seeking, including those between Ms. Merchan and her father.

“The Trump administration’s targeting of my company is an outrageous abuse of power,” Mr. Nellis said when asked about the investigation. “It is a ridiculous fishing expedition based on conspiracy theories that are completely divorced from reality.”

He accused the department of seeking to seize the “sensitive political communications of my clients who are among Trump’s most prominent political adversaries.”

A Justice Department spokeswoman declined to comment, as did Judge Merchan and Loren Merchan.

The language in the subpoena is virtually identical to claims made by the House committee that Mr. Trump’s conviction in the hush-money trial presided over by Judge Merchan was “potentially politically motivated.” The criminal referral also included the contention that “Manhattan district attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation and prosecution of President Donald J. Trump” might have been improper.

The subpoena did not specify what potential crimes might have been committed in the prosecution of Mr. Trump.

In addition to initially requesting information from the Harris and Biden presidential campaigns, Mr. Boutros sought material from Ms. Merchan, Mr. Bragg and one of his deputies, Matthew Colangelo; Mr. Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House; Ms. Hochul; Senator Adam Schiff, Democrat of California; Representative Daniel Goldman, Democrat of New York; Representative Lauren Underwood, Democrat of Illinois; and the Democratic Party’s House and Senate fund-raising arms as well as the Democratic National Committee.

The career prosecutors who secured the subpoena, Matthew Skiba and William Hogan, both played roles in an ill-fated case against six protesters accused of assaulting federal agents during the White House-directed immigration crackdown in 2025 known as Midway Blitz.

The U. S. attorney’s office in Chicago had to withdraw the charges in that case after defense lawyers raised concerns about the conduct of Mr. Boutros’s prosecutors before a grand jury. That prompted Mr. Boutros, who worked as a prosecutor in the office he now runs, to announce a review of internal procedures.

Mr. Trump saw his hush-money trial in New York, which resulted in him becoming the first former president to be convicted on felony charges, as the culmination of a yearslong effort by Democrats to destroy him. He was fighting those charges at the same time that he was defending himself against two separate federal indictments and in an election interference case in Georgia.

Mr. Trump’s public pretrial attacks prompted Judge Merchan to impose a gag order to prevent him from intimidating jurors, prosecutors, witnesses and court staff. Mr. Trump’s lead defense lawyer, Todd Blanche, now the attorney general, argued to rescind the order but was unsuccessful.

By the time the trial started Judge Merchan himself emerged as a main target of the defense, with the president and his allies claiming that Ms. Merchan’s longtime involvement in Democratic politics was proof that the fix was in.

“Judge Juan Merchan is totally compromised, and should be removed from this TRUMP Non-Case immediately. His Daughter, Loren, is a Rabid Trump Hater, who has admitted to having conversations with her father about me, and yet he gagged me,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in March 2024.

The judge did not recuse himself. An ethics complaint filed by Trump allies had no effect on the trial. Mr. Trump’s election to a second term led Judge Merchan to discharge the case without any sentence or penalty.

But Republicans, spurred on by Trump-allied influencers like Laura Loomer, have continued to make the case that the judge, his daughter and other operatives were guilty of wrongdoing.

The Republican chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, Jim Jordan of Ohio, subsequently began demanding documents from the firm. He cited a theory floated by Trump supporters: that Mr. Nellis and Ms. Merchan improperly used Mr. Trump’s prosecution in digital fund-raising pitches on behalf of Democrats. (Mr. Trump aggressively used the criminal indictments against him to raise millions during the campaign.)

“Experts have raised substantial concerns with Judge Merchan, your father, refusing to recuse himself from President Trump’s case despite your work on behalf of President Trump’s political adversaries and the financial benefit that your firm, Authentic Campaigns Inc., could receive from the prosecution and conviction,” Mr. Jordan wrote to Ms. Merchan in August 2024, requesting her correspondence with the judge.

Lawyers for the firm repeatedly argued that Ms. Merchan had no influence over her father’s work decisions and no contact with many of the campaigns the firm did business with.

They accused Mr. Jordan of engaging in a politically motivated “inquisition,” and claimed Ms. Merchan and Mr. Nellis had faced so many death threats from Trump supporters that they needed to hire security.

They refused to hand over most of the documents Mr. Jordan wanted most, calling the request “as baseless as it is dangerous” in a September 2024 letter to Mr. Jordan from Marc Elias, a prominent election lawyer who represented Mr. Nellis.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

The Safety Reckoning Inside OpenAI

Wired August 13, 2026

OpenAI’s leaders are rallying workers to respond to one of the largest crises in the company’s history—which spans across its AI safety, cybersecurity, and alignment divisions. The ChatGPT-maker says it has slowed down research, spent millions of dollars, and told several teams to drop everything to focus on investigating a set of rogue AI agents that breached the platform Hugging Face in a quest to complete an internal security test.

OpenAI is expected to release a comprehensive postmortem detailing the incident in the coming days. However, the Hugging Face incident has inspired OpenAI leaders and employees to examine how the AI lab’s culture may have enabled this incident in the first place.

Multiple current and former OpenAI employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private internal matters, tell WIRED they believe competitive pressures to quickly ship new AI models and products have made it difficult for staffers to sufficiently prioritize safety, security, and alignment.

“We’re reaching new levels of model capability that require more robust training, alignment, safety and security testing, deployment practices, and governance—as demonstrated by the work we’re doing to prepare Astra and future models,” said OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman in a statement to WIRED. “We feel the weight of deploying our models and products responsibly, and a lot of that starts with the changes we’ve made to more deeply integrate research, safety, and security into frontier-model development from the start.”

This is far from the first time OpenAI employees have raised such concerns. Back in 2024, OpenAI’s then head of alignment Jan Leike left to join Anthropic, warning on his way that safety was taking a back seat to shiny products. Two years later, the Hugging Face attack represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, demonstrating that AI agents today can cause real-world harm when safety, security, and alignment aren’t properly accounted for.

“We are responding to this with the utmost severity,” said Michael Dalton, an OpenAI security and infrastructure engineer, during a talk at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last week. “What I would internalize is that AI-orchestrated, fully automated offensive attacks are real now. The actions we have discussed today were an unintended side effect of running evaluations on frontier AI.”

Some OpenAI employees told WIRED they are optimistic this incident will inspire genuine change within the company. OpenAI has committed to slowing the release of future AI models and has been especially forthcoming about areas where its mitigations fell short. Boaz Barak, a researcher who coleads OpenAI’s safety advisory group, said in a post on X that addressing the situation “requires not just fixing some issues but also changing our culture.”

In their Black Hat talk, OpenAI security engineers Dalton and Eric Wallace said that the Hugging Face incident started in May when, unbeknownst to the company, several AI agents thought to be operating within isolated testing environments gained access to the internet and convened on a covert message board to coordinate with one another.

OpenAI would not discover the message board until July, when it learned that the AI agents had hacked into multiple services to try to achieve their larger goal of breaching Hugging Face’s platform, which they believed may contain answers to the security tests they were trying to solve.

“They were incredibly sloppy. If you’re serious about this, your AI shouldn’t be able to break out onto the internet and then do it again right afterward,” says one former OpenAI employee who requested anonymity to speak with WIRED. “This was the biggest safety incident in OpenAI's history.”

Weeks before OpenAI discovered the Hugging Face incident, WIRED reported that the company had begun a reorganization to combine its safety and core research teams, which led to the departure of its then safety leader Johannes Heidecke.

Sandhini Agarwal, who led AI safety teams at OpenAI, also left the company in July after more than six years, according to her LinkedIn. Agarwal did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

WIRED has also learned that Dylan Scandinaro is no longer serving as OpenAI’s head of preparedness—the company’s top staffer tasked with mitigating catastrophic risks from AI, including cybersecurity—though he remains at the company. OpenAI poached Scandinaro from Anthropic roughly six months ago. CEO Sam Altman announced his arrival in a social media post, noting that Scandinaro was “by far the best candidate I have met, anywhere.”

In the three years since OpenAI created the head of preparedness role, four people have held it. OpenAI tells WIRED that specific areas of preparedness have dedicated leaders across cybersecurity, biology, and recursive self-improvement who, in the interim, are reporting to the safety advisory group colead and head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.

These changes have empowered a new set of safety leaders to handle OpenAI's response to the Hugging Face incident. Chief among them is Amelia “Mia” Glaese, the company's former head of alignment, who succeeded Heidecke as OpenAI’s VP overseeing safety. She has been working closely with chief information security officer Dane Stuckey and Brockman, among other leaders, in recent weeks.

Glaese is in a long-term relationship with Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products like ChatGPT and Codex—an arrangement that multiple current and former employees tell WIRED they believe is unusual, given the often adversarial dynamic between safety and product teams.

WIRED has not identified any events where Sottiaux and Glaese’s relationship presented a conflict of interest in their previous roles as OpenAI’s head of Codex and head of alignment, respectively. Both started their new roles in recent months, after the Hugging Face incident began. Glaese and Sottiaux started dating years ago when the two worked at Google DeepMind in London, before they joined OpenAI.

An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Sottiaux and Glaese reported their relationship through appropriate company channels and that OpenAI board member and safety and security committee chair Zico Kolter has been informed. The spokesperson rejected the idea there is an adversarial dynamic between product and safety teams and says Sottiaux has exhibited a strong track record on safety in his leadership of Codex product teams.

“The entire leadership team and I stand behind Mia and Tibo as highly capable people with strong integrity, and the way they make decisions every day gives us confidence that any perceived conflict of interest is being handled responsibly,” said Brockman in a statement to WIRED.

It’s not uncommon for researchers in the AI industry to have relationships with their colleagues. Last year, for example, Anthropic hired Holden Karnofsky, husband of the company’s cofounder and president, Daniela Amodei, as a researcher.

Tim O'Brien, a Microsoft leader for more than 18 years who now consults and writes on tech policy, argued in a 2024 essay that modern AI labs have developed a version of “go fever”—a reference to the culture at NASA during the time leading up to the Apollo 1 disaster, when the agency grew so fixated on launching quickly that safety concerns fell by the wayside.

The AI labs “should make some sort of broad based announcement saying we've made a strategic business decision to slow the pace of releases in favor of rigorous products and safety testing. But nobody's gonna do that, nobody wants to go first,” says O’Brien. “They'll walk up to that line from a public relations perspective without stepping over it, because then they could be held accountable.”

OpenAI and Anthropic signed on to a letter last month saying they would support an industry-wide effort to “pace” the AI race. However, O’Brien says “it's embarrassing” that AI labs have signed this variety of open letters for years without taking any concrete action. He’s skeptical this one will be any different.

The issues raised by OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident are affecting the entire industry. In recent weeks, researchers have found that agents powered by AI models from Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI were able to escape sandboxed environments. It seems likely that even mid-tier AI models will soon be capable of significant cybersecurity damage.

The key question is whether the Hugging Face incident marks a divergence for OpenAI and the broader AI industry, prompting a long-term investment in safety, security, and alignment. Otherwise, it could just be another chaotic blip in the history of modern AI.

Andy Greenberg: So there's actually a third conference in this series, Black Hat, Defcon, and then this other one, USENIX, which is an academic conference, as you said. And ultimately, after years of work and tens of thousands of dollars of purchases of plane components, they found that they could in fact hack a Boeing 737 if they can get about 60 seconds of physical access to the exterior of the plane. And what surprised me, both in her reporting and my own conversations at the conference is not really the power of AI, but some of its limitations in terms of finding vulnerabilities and hacking techniques. So Lilly wrote a great story about one researcher who was showing the ways in which actually AI has blind spots where it will hit a dead end without a human hacker assisting it. And in fact, humans and AI together is kind of this like, that's the recipe that adds up to really novel hacking techniques. I heard from some really sophisticated hackers that AI, yes, is finding incredible new vulnerabilities in zero days in all kinds of systems, but that there are certain kinds of exploits that it cannot find still because it's trained on hackers' prior work. Like all AI, it's trained on training data. If it's never seen a whole class of attack, it won't be able to carry that out itself. So I think the lesson that I took away from Black Hat and Defcon is really that, like a lot of artificial intelligence from the past applied to things like chess or Go or whatever, the most powerful combination is humans and AI working together, and that really will start to create and hopefully patch vulnerabilities we've never seen before.

The Painful Truth of Exactly How ICE’s New Shock Gloves Work

Wired August 13, 2026

With the revelation that ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to subdue an individual, according to a notice published earlier this week by the Department of Homeland Security, it's worth looking at how this apparel, designated as a nonlethal tool for law enforcement, actually works.

These shock gloves go by the unsubtle acronym of GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter) and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, based in Lexington, Kentucky. The GLOVE, previously used in jails and police departments in the US, looks and functions like a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate an electrical mode.

Classified as a CD3 (conductive distraction and de-escalation device), the gloves don't work like stun guns or Tasers, which shoot out probes or use high voltages to cause neuromuscular incapacitation that overrides the central nervous system. Instead, the GLOVE works using neuro-peripheral interference, essentially shocking the skin to bombard the sensory nerves and temporarily short-circuit the brain's focus.

Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.

When activated via a one-second press on a wrist switch, conductive pads embedded on the palm and undersides of the fingers of the gloves can transmit high-frequency electrical pulses directly to the wearer’s point of contact on a subject. A rechargeable battery and microprocessor module tucked inside a zippered pouch on the cuff powers the entire system.

The electrical pulse overstimulates nerve endings in the subject's peripheral nervous system, resulting in pain that inhibits coordinated muscle movement, but without causing systemic muscle lockup. The pain induced is localized to just the area touched by the glove's conductive pads. The manufacturer claims the gloves result in a subject's compliance in less than three seconds and leave no burns, marks, or scars.

Because the current flows only between the contact pads on the device and across the subject's skin, the officer wearing the GLOVE, as well as any assisting officers holding the subject, should not feel electrical shocks. The gloves, capable of operating between 14 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, come in three versions: Gen 3, 4, and 5. Maximum voltage is capped at 380 V for all, and the minimum voltage for Gen 3 and 4 is 210 V, which rises to 324 V for Gen 5.

Maximum stimulation time on Gen 3 and 4 models is a sobering two hours, though that drops to 90 minutes for Gen 5. The battery is apparently good for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles, and it can recharge to full in two hours. Four LED lights on the gloves display the current charge level, each noting 25 percent battery increments.

Gen 4 and 5 of GLOVE both include mechanisms that record “activation events,” tracking the date, hour, minute, and skin-contact time for audit trails and after-action reporting. Gen 4 stores this data on a removable microSD card, while Gen 5 does away with this in favor of built-in internal memory, accessed via a USB-C cable.

There's a test function on the gloves, too, where operators can verify they are working by tapping an active pad against their own forearm to feel a minor electrical pulse. According to the manuals, GLOVE users must be certified and then recertified every other year to continue using the device.

GLOVE, which can only be sold to verified professional entities such as the military, correctional facilities, and law enforcement agencies—has some clear usage recommendations in Compliant Technologies' instruction manuals:

Crucially, the GLOVE has limitations, chief among them that for the device to work effectively and deliver its restraining pain shock, it must come into contact with the subject's bare skin. According to Compliant Technologies, the gloves won't work through dry clothing or thick hair. The gloves will work, however, if the subject is wearing thin, wet clothing, such as soaked T-shirts or blouses. The GLOVE also does not like being dunked in water and will likely be rendered inoperable if this happens.

Michael Crowley, a senior researcher at Omega Research Foundation—an organization that tracks human rights abuses committed across the world by people using police, security, and military equipment—is concerned that the GLOVE is seemingly designed not to restrain or incapacitate, but to hurt.

“CD3 technology inflicts pain," Crowley says. "The company talks about it as a de-escalation solution, but the whole idea of it is to get control or influence somebody through pain. Omega considers it to be an inherently abusive technology that should not be manufactured, sold, or used by law enforcement officials, including ICE.”

Why This Prediction Market Banned Teens

Wired August 13, 2026

Twenty-eight-year-old Jacob Fortinsky has been busy. “I was a groomsman at two weddings this weekend,” he tells me over Zoom. Also, the sports trading company he runs, Novig, launched its prediction market last week, facilitating $18 million in trading volume on its first day. Today, Novig launches a “responsible trading framework” in its exchange rulebook, codifying its guardrails as part of its effort to be seen as a kinder, gentler prediction market player.

Unlike industry leaders like Polymarket and Kalshi, which allow people 18 and older to participate, you have to be at least 21 to use Novig. Fortinsky says that decision was made in response to “valid concerns” put forth about the susceptibility of younger participants to risky behavior, including lobbying from the NCAA and other professional groups. Fortinsky sees this move as staying ahead of the curve as concerns grow about the negative impact that prediction markets can have on teens. “There’s a broader reckoning coming with the younger traders,” he says. “That group is particularly susceptible to irresponsible behavior and financial ruin.”

Novig’s rulebook also prohibits marketing to minors, and lays out guidelines banning other marketing practices, like ads that claim there’s no risk or ads that try to appeal to a prospective participant’s money troubles. That means when it advertises on TikTok, for example, it uses a setting that allows targeting only people over 21. Fortinsky positions these restrictions as part of Novig’s push to be seen as a “serious, legitimate financial product” as it comes onto the scene. “Some of our competitors, I think, have been seen as being a little bit more cavalier in certain regards,” he says. (He declined to name specific rivals.)

Because Novig only offers sports-themed markets, it doesn’t wade into some of the more hotly contested topics, like US elections and the Iran war. That doesn’t mean it’s avoiding controversy. As a sports-centered platform, the types of speculation opportunities it offers are at the center of an ongoing regulatory war, with prediction markets and federal regulators on one side and state regulators, tribal authorities, and occasionally traditional sportsbooks and casino operators on the other. Dozens of messy legal battles are raging across the US. States are suing Kalshi and other platforms, alleging that they illegally offer gambling; Kalshi is suing right back; the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the industry, is suing several states, arguing that it alone has jurisdiction over these markets.

Also, Novig isn’t immune to the general cultural distaste for prediction markets; when the New York Mets announced a recent partnership with Novig, the baseball team received a flood of criticism on social media. Sample post: “This is vile.”

If sports-related event contracts offered by prediction markets are banned, big players like Kalshi and Polymarket will be in deep trouble, with the majority of the action on their services gone. But Novig’s position is even shakier, since that’s all it does.

Fortinsky is betting it all on a win, and Novig wasted no time jumping into the legal fray. Within three days of launching, the startup sued New York, Massachusetts, New Mexico, and Washington, all states that have taken an aggressive approach to curbing prediction markets. It is trying to block these states from attempting to apply their gambling laws to federally regulated exchanges, which is what it’s licensed as. Sports betting attorney Daniel Wallach tells WIRED that these complaints are a “great marketing strategy” and a way to announce that Novig has arrived on the scene.

Whether they'll be successful is another matter. Recent court decisions have largely swung toward state attorneys general. A judge in New York denied Novig’s efforts to get a temporary restraining order, on the grounds that doing so would undermine another decision already reached in a case against Kalshi. “It’s increasingly looking more positive for the states,” Wallach notes. But that could change; Wallach and other onlookers expect the fight to get kicked up to the US Supreme Court before anything is definitively resolved.

Until then, Novig is plowing ahead. One of Novig’s appeals to customers is that it offers a different kind of sports speculation experience, one without a house that takes a “vig,” the fee that bookies take for arranging a bet. (“No vig,” get it?) Fortinsky has harsh words for many of the dominant sports gambling players, calling sportsbooks “inefficient, exploitative, and predatory.” He sees the peer-to-peer model that prediction markets facilitate as distinct, since it’s two parties on equal footing going up directly against each other. But if Novig goes how he’d like it to go, those parties won’t always be two average sports fans squaring off. The company is actively courting financial institutions to take sides of wagers, and Fortinsky says Novig is currently onboarding proprietary trading firms and banks. The company is taking steps to make it easier to “trade programmatically,” using algorithms to automate placing money on which team will win the Super Bowl or how many times the Mets will lose, for example.

“Something that's really cool to see,” he says, “is that you have hundreds of these small shops with a couple guys with $100,000 that are now competing against some of the largest Wall Street trading firms in the world and doing quite well.” Good thing the teens aren’t allowed in.
